Hatchlings
by Nathan McKnight


Book I: Flotsam
Chapter 00: Darknesses
It was a new kind of darkness--a shock, for I had come to know darknesses so well. After all these dozens of fives and twos, I'd come to recognize in an instant whether I was waking to the common darknesses of a midnight beating, or the darkness of a burlap sack, or the comfortable darkness of my felted blanket on the packed dirt floor. Those were common darknesses. There were uncommon darknesses too. The forced march in the Siberian night, the smothering darkness of a wet pillow, or the throbbing darkness of a cracked skull. But this new darkness, this was different altogether. This was a queasy, lolling and dripping wet, pierced by thumb-thick shafts of light, sprawled against cardboard box corners kind of darkness. 
With newness, fear. With fear, questions. Should I alert my captors that something felt wrong? Or should I shut up and endure? Endurance was so often the only choice, but when changes happened as they occasionally would, it was hard to tell if the Yakuts wanted me to speak up or shut up.
I touched my head--it was bleeding. Had I already received a beating and would be beaten again for forgetting the previous beating? I touched my feet. They were not bound, and that is what made me speak up.
“Hello,” I said in Yakut, “Hello, my feet are not bound. Will you bind my feet?” 
No answer.
“Hello, sirs. I need to be bound. Do you wish to bind my feet, and hands?”
No answer. 
Wrongness compounded wrongness, and I knew I had to do something. So I curled into a ball among the boxes and let myself be rocked by the lolling dark space.
            #
After what seemed like hours, I determined that the I was floating. Slowly, the rocking sensation had resolved into a clear back and forth, and it wasn’t just the throb of my head. The room, the boxes, everything was somehow buoying on gentle waves. There was a light lapping of water, and behind that sound, there was the sound of shallow breathing. I knew that particular breathing. My blood seemed to slow in my veins, afraid to move for fear of waking the Koryak. I tried to quiet my mind, but it would not quiet.
I must get the attention of one of the Yakuts, and I must do it without waking the Koryak. If they saw my untethered feet, there might be an argument and perhaps the Korkyak would storm off. Or perhaps he would take his anger out on me. But the presence of a Manchary or Ayhal would temper him. Moving carefully away from the Koryak’s subtle breathing, I felt for a ladder, a staircase, a rope. But there was nothing. Just boxes. I looked up at the shafts of light. When my eyes managed to focus, I could tell they were coming from small holes in the ceiling not far above.
I stumbled over the boxes and didn’t get far before encountering a ribbed composite wall. The ribs were sloped the wrong way for climbing, but I managed to pull myself up by the fingernails of my left hand, and almost immediately hit my head on the ceiling, knocking myself back into the boxes. I froze, bracing myself for a beating, but there was none. I stayed still until I could hear the Koryak’s breathing again under the pounding of my heart. He never slept so soundly. Was this a trick? Was he letting me get myself into trouble so that when he pounced, he would indulge his cruelty just that much more? Was I digging my own grave with every move?
I was alone with the Koryak. I had to reach the Yakuts. 
In spite of my fear, I tried again. This time, more slowly, I pulled myself up, ignoring the bleeding of my cracked and callused palms as I struggled to hold on to the little flaws and formation-marks on the composite wall. I reached a hand up and felt the low ceiling. There was a rail running along its seam with the wall. Leveraging myself was a triumph of will against my scarred and malnourished body, but I could just bring my eyes to one of the glimmering holes. It was no bigger than my pinkie finger, and when my eye got used to the brightness, I could make out nothing through it except cloud-brushed skyscape. I felt the edge of the hole with my finger. It was a bullet hole.
I had a flash of memory. Shots had been fired. The clickety-clack-whump of bullets ricocheting off composite and burying themselves in cardboard. I remembered somebody muttering in a language I couldn't understand--was it the smoky purr of Cantonese? I remembered a young Chinese man knocking me with the but of a microwave rifle. 
Rain dripped into my eye through the bullet hole, dripped down my face. My body was beginning to shake from exertion. Besides the few occasions when the Yakuts made me carry their packs in the early days, and of course the frequent beatings and other tortures, this was by far the most strenuous activity I had undertaken for years. It felt terrible--it felt wonderful. My muscles aching with exertion, my ankles open to the air instead of knocking together between ropes. For the first time, I felt... Well, it must be joy. Joy tinged with fear, of course, as all emotions were so tinged--but still astonishing, unfamiliar yet recognizable, joy.
The rainwater seeped into my mouth through my cracked lips, and into my flesh through the cracks in my lips. It stung terribly, and I tasted it. It was briny. Not rainwater, then--sea water. And I remembered. 
I had been on a sea train, and I was supposed to be released. 
Released!
I brought my mouth up to the bullet hole.
“Hello!” I rasped, lips chafing against the sharp edges of the composite. “Sirs, hello!”
My legs were quaking fiercely and one of my feet slipped. In the second before my other foot slipped, I reset my hold on the rail, and when my legs went, I swung. No no no, I thought. Don’t let me fall and die. My recurrent death wish had been evaporated by shafts of brilliant light. I knew the boxes were not far below me, but the darkness below my dangling feet felt like infinity--another new kind of darkness. I grasped for my life and kicked my legs in the open air. Tears streamed down my cheeks. No!
My hands slipped, flailing in air. But I didn't fall into the infinite void. I was back in the boxes, heart racing, penetrated through with fear, blind and in pain. But my mind was alive--through the pain and confusion, I focussed on one thing: Release. 
I sifted my memories. The last thing I remembered was being let out of a cargo container--that must be what I was in now--and allowed to walk around on the deck of a ship; a sea train. The marine air had been salty and rank, and I found that in my captivity, I had be come an agoraphobe, the vast emptiness of waves in all directions. But the open daylight had been a blessing, and the warm breeze had been an impossible delight after so long in chilly Sakha.
My guards had been a Yakut and three Russians, and they had seemed to be having skipping railgun shots off the translucent sunlit waves, as others tried to vaporize the rails in flight with maser blasts, which usually ended in geysers of steam erupting from the hummocky wavescape. The size of the sea train had been astonishing, terrifying. The barge we were on had stretched perhaps a quarter mile, and I could count at least three more attached barges in front and two behind, all of them stacked high with cargo containers. When I had first been captured, I only knew sea trains to be two or three barges long, and not nearly so large. Much must have changed. I reveled in the memory of a hint of a taste of freedom.
Absorbed, I lay fetal among the boxes. 
Movement. 
I scrambled, moving in a direction I thought was away from the sound, but as soon as I did, I was on top of the Koryak. His sweaty shirt stunk, but his muscles were slack. He slouched against one of the composite walls, collapsed among the crushed cardboard. I jumped back, and hit another wall, felt along it, tripping on boxes and clawing at the composite all the way. In short succession, I turned three corners and found myself back where the Koryak rested. This container was small, with boxes piled deep enough that I couldn’t tell if there was a floor at all.
Fighting queasy terror, I ran my hands gingerly over the Koryak’s pockets, looking for a gun, a knife, something. The promise of freedom had whet my appetite for survival. I had forgotten that I could want anything at all. The Koryak's pockets were empty. He wore a tool belt, but the only thing on it was a tape measure. I took it, feeling for sharp edges, and briefly flicking a built-in laser level. The sudden flash of red startled me. There was a belt clip, and in desperation, I climbed the wall again with the tape measure clipped to my threadbare jeans. I propped myself in place again, arching my back and pulling until my muscles strained, then swinging the tape measure hard against the bullet hole. Nothing happened, but an echo that seemed to tumble around the container as the we bobbed. I scratched at the hole with the corner of the tape measure, and managed to get the belt clip to catch the rough edge. I worked at it until my arms and legs trembled, and still I persisted. At last, I managed to get the clip all the way through the hole, but I couldn’t yank it hard enough to tear the composite.
So, I put all my weight on it, quickly grabbing with both hands and letting my legs swing. I fell almost immediately and I could feel my skin tear and crack and leak warm blood even before I landed with a crunch on the boxes. 
I looked up and saw that I had torn a hand-sized flap into the composite. I gritted my teeth in the closest thing to a smile I could manage, then felt around until I found the tape measure again. When I stopped to bend the belt clip back to a useable position, I heard that the Koryak’s breathing had changed. Shallower, quieter. 
More in control. 
With a sudden rush of adrenaline, I flicked the laser level towards where I thought his eyes would be.
He chuckled and lunged.
I covered my face and swung the tape measure hard at his temple, but he was on top of me and I couldn’t land a solid blow. His knees were in my ribs, and he shouted in the Koryak language. I bit his arm as hard as I could, not stopping when I tasted blood. He groaned and pulled back, giving me just enough distance and just enough time to slash his face with the ragged metal belt clip. His breathing was labored, but he didn't scream. I did it again, feeling the rough cutting of his flesh with satisfaction, then again, and he was backing away. He hit a wall and slipped and I used the opportunity to fall on him, jamming both my knees into his groin and taking a bash at his face. I kept bashing him with the heavy tape measure over and over again, and with each tear of flesh, each crunch of bone, I remembered the burns, the cuts, the fingernails, and I hit him harder each time until I was bashing nothing but greasy tissue into soaked cardboard.
I shuddered. I had seen such acts often enough, but it was the first time I killed another human being. 
My fingers tightened on hair and skin and blood and I stood, pulling the gore away from its source, then I flung it down, wiped my hands on my pants, and climbed the wall for the last time. I didn’t care if I had to swim home. Damn the Koryak. I was free.
At the top of the composite wall, I stuck my arm through the flap I had ripped, feeling cold saltwater bite my wounds. I pulled hard on the flap, and it widened so I could get another hand through, then another arm. I felt a rail on the outside surface and grabbed it with both hands, pulling my body through the hole, letting the composite slice into the skin of my belly, thigh, shins. It could have gutted me for all I cared. The sun was blinding, but I was out and crouching atop the container and I felt around as I tried to strain my eyes open. There container's shiny outer surface was wet and slippery, and I slid a short distance, day-blind, and tripped over another rail.
I tumbled and splashed, and found myself underwater. Now, despite the saltwater sting and the burn of the sun, I willed my eyes open and reached for the shadow of the container, grabbing the rail and clinging tight. I pulled myself above water, folded my arms around the rail, and held on for life. 
When my eyes adjusted, I surveyed my predicament. There was nothing but the container's red enamel and open sea all around. The great bulk swayed with the lapping waves. I lifted myself on top of it again. 
It had been upended, floating vertically, and I crouched on its narrow end, looking around at open sea and open sky. 
Fourteen years as a hostage, and this is how it ends.
I was alone--afloat in the open ocean.
But I was free.
#
It’s hard to say how long I was sitting on that container. Everything of my former life seemed entombed in that cherry red sepulcher, the great gash in its composite skin matching the gashes in my own, a nastily-torn umbilical. I roused from my half-sleep half-daze as the sun set over the craggy waves. It was so beautiful I cried.
I stared at the spot where the sun had set for an apparent infinity, watching stars rain almost imperceptibly over the horizon. The sea became choppier as I stared into the night. Rain began to rain down, washing the layers of filth from my skin. I had had no shower in…Months? Years? 
Ayhal had told me they would allow me to wash before I reached home. I grimaced. So they had. 
As I rocked in the rain, I let my mind wander. Memories were returning in earnest now.
The sea train was meant to be my ride back home. Manchary and Ayhal said they were trading me for prisoners held in Moscow. My life was worth sixteen prisoners, they’d said, both triumphant and disdainful. I had dared to chuckle. My rapport with the Yakuts had long since mellowed, and when they were around, I had dared to show joviality because I could. Not like earlier on, when the conflict was still fresh and the youthful 'freedom fighters' blazed zealous. 
At one point early on, they had decided they were going to entertain themselves with exotic torture techniques.
They laughed and whispered horrors to me as they shopped online for Thai bamboo. They bought the seeds, and taunted me for weeks about how they were going to weight me down and let the fast-growing stalks grow through my torso. An excruciating death, it haunted the dreams I had in what little sleep I got back then. In the end, the seeds had refused to grow in the soggy Siberian soil. I had giggled silently at night for weeks after that in my cell. They only caught me giggling once, and that was worth all the nails on my right hand to them--and to me. You take humor where you can.
I used to talk to them when I could, mostly to practice my Yakut or Russian, but companionship is hard to come by in wartime, and my chats had the effect of easing my captivity sometimes. I suppose that’s why their directorate or overlords, or whomever they answered to had hired the Koryak eventually. 
There was no befriending the Koryak. We didn’t have a common tongue, and he had no interest in talking, apparently, to anybody.
The Manchary had told me he’d been a reindeer herder until the reindeer could no longer weather the warming steppes. Strange to know so little about someone you killed. But I supposed that was usually the way of things. 
The seaborne rain was calming to a tiny pitter, and I let myself sleep.
#
I awoke feeling like I was falling into a swamp, grasping at a vine that kept slipping out of my hand. When I realized the vine was the rail and the swamp was several inches of water running in thick rivulets into the gash in the container, I panicked. I slipped on the polished surface, and tried to get to the higher end of the rail, but it was no use. My body had been blocking the flow, and when I moved, seawater poured as a torrent into the container's maw. 
In moments, the high end had reached the water line, and my ankles and butt were in water. The hole was completely submerged now, and I could see bursts of air shooting out as the huge container sunk beneath me. I held on until I was up to my waist in water, then tried to float, but just at that point, the whole thing descended so fast out from under me that I was pulled after it in the undertow. This was the end, I thought, feeling the weight of the water compress me. The dim glow of dawn receded above me, lost in bubbles and turbulence, and I tried to gasp but only took in water. I was going to drown.
As the surface darkened and I felt the pressure close in on me, something punched me from below, hitting my body with the force of a brick wall, all corners and sharp edges. The impact was so forceful that it made a shockwave of sound that felt as though it would pierce my eardrums. Orangey sunlight appeared suddenly before my eyes, and I was forced again above the surface of the water. I flailed, coughing and gasping for air, and I tried to paddle, but my arms just hit cardboard. All around me, an oil slick of shoeboxes, buoying me. I floated on them, spread eagle, coughing the water from my lungs.
I was woosey, and I must have lapsed into and out of consciousness. I know day and night passed at least twice, but I could not be sure of how long it had been. I felt dizzy, cracked lips and muttering like a drunkard in the moments of consciousness, but mostly I slept.
#
The growling of my stomach woke me. 
The boxes had turned to a slimy foamy mush. My body ached with hunger and thirst. There was nothing but shoes and cardboard pulp. I tried to eat some of that. But it was pasty and fibrous and coated my tongue. I had to rinse with the little seawater I could squeeze out of a handful of the mushy box residue, and the effort left my mouth dry and sore.



Chapter 00: Salvage
When the old man found me, he prodded me. And in my stupor, I asked if he was real. He put his hand on my shoulder, and I flinched, but all he did was to hoist me onto the little dinghy he towed behind his jet-ski. I looked around with my cracked eyelids and gummy vision, and saw that he had perched me atop a slimy pile of Nikes. I chuckled, and was out again.
#
A dribbling of earthy-green flavor roused me. It took me a moment to realize it was water, but by that time, my body had already instinctively lapped it up. The old man was using some sort of plant roots to dip and dribble into my mouth from a large algae-laced jar.
He offered the root wad to me, saying “De-saleen,” and I dipped it myself, hesitantly at first, then greedily, sating an infinite thirst over and again until I was glutted on the delicious green water.
He offered some sort of seafood jerky, covered in a white powder, and I took it, touching it to the tip of my tongue. The powder was acrid, acid, metallic and wrong-salty. Evidently noticing my trepidation, he handed me a little condiment packet.
“Tekas bah-bah-koo,” he said, “Mmm-mmm.”
He gave a rotten-toothed chuckle, and I almost smiled. I squeezed the barbecue sauce on the salted squid and ate as much as I could stand. My stomach was full of water, but still churning with hunger. It had been so long since I had eaten.
The food tasted wrong, but I knew I had to eat something.
I lay on smooth wooden planks, and I felt nauseous, as if the whole world were swaying. I looked around; there were improvised shanties in all directions. Men, women, and children peered from most of the doors. These were homes, studded with bubble wrap and Styrofoam and industrial garbage. The sky was clear blue over their rooves, no sign of larger development. The houses were connected by wooden plank bridges and lashed together with replastic ropes. 
I had seen such curiosity towards westerners before—we were a rare breed, and getting rarer—but otherwise, it was like no rural village I had ever visited. There wasn’t a single patch of open space; the houses tumbled over one another like a densely packed cityscape. But this was not urban shantytown. It was deathly quiet save for the occasional squawk of a seagull.
As I ate, I stared at the old man. At first, I had thought him a Yakut wearing some kind of traditional cap. But the patterns were wrong…fine threadwork in delicate filigree, tracing elaborate geometries around what looked like an Islamic crescent-and-star. Moreover, his face was wrong; brown-dark instead of ruddy, sunbeaten-leathery instead of cold-bitten leathery.
When he spoke, there was no longer a question.
            “Ya mirá yo con Noe. Noe, Noe,” he said, tapping his chest with bunched fingers.
He repeated the whole exercise several times before I recognized he was speaking some form of Spanish. I hadn’t spoken the language in decades, but I had grown up in the Bronx, and the words came to my lips without hesitation.
“Mi nombre es Lucius. ¿Quién eres tú?” Who are you?
“Ya mirá yo con Noe, soy Banguingui.”
“¿Que?”
“Baa--ngui-ngui,” he said it as if speaking to a child. “Esta gitano del mar. Ya mir--ah…mi nombre es Noa.”
Gitano del mar, I thought. Sea gypsy.
My stomach began to contract of its own accord. The sea gypsy—Noe—grabbed me under the arms and dragged me to the edge of the nearest walkway. He was ancient and stringy, but strong. His muscles felt like two granite bannisters under mine. As he laid me out on my belly, I wretched fish-tinged algae water over the edge into sloshing seafoam a few feet below. Noe braced himself expertly against a taut rope, stretching a leg through the gap and flicking his foot in water to rinse off the vomit.
He left me alone and waved off the others, and I lay there for long enough to notice late afternoon fade into early evening. I heaved a lot at first, then less and less frequently until I felt wrung-out, empty but for a knot of muscle that was my stomach, almost as hard as Noe’s arms.
When the slow rocking of the whole village slowly became predictable, and when I was finally certain it wasn’t just me, and when I was sure I could, I stood. I seemed to myself to be an emaciated cadaver, weeks beyond death. Yet I stood, doddered.
On one side, the village rose towards a boxy, spire-like structure. On the other, walkways extended between shacks and shanties and, strangely, amid all the roughshod architecture, there stood boats of all sizes and styles, embedded in the village, built into the houses--houses built on, around, and through the boats. The whole structure creaked and lurched subtly. Some of the boats were new, but most were weather-streaked, bubbling rusty or sunbaked, crumbly fiberglass mesh. Sea birds squawked about the masts and corrugated fiberglass roofs.
Noe appeared from one of the boats, a formerly-luxury yacht whose bow jutted through a large structure that could've been straight out of the American Old West. 
The cobbled-together island seemed built to surround a crescent of open water with small round objects floating in it. I couldn’t tell what they were from here, but they seemed to have plants growing in them. On the broad boardwalk that bordered the tiny artificial bay, there was a small but sturdy-looking brass ship’s bell mounted atop a shiny and equally sturdy brass post. A young girl, barely more than a toddler, climbed the post with two hands behind it and her feet almost flat against the sparkling metal. She rang the bell louder that I would have expected possible for such a small bell, and such a small girl.
He took me by the elbow, and walked me into the yacht. The smell of campfire tinged with burning plastics hit my nose.
A gathering was taking place around a central fire. Smoke pooled in the high ceiling area, and from the deep chocolaty surfaces, I assumed this must have been used as a meeting place for a very long time. Noe introduced me to a young man in a perfectly clean white daishiki, tallish and sharply chiseled, obviously muscular despite the loose clothing, but with the same features and weather-battered look as Noe. He wore a similar Moslem hat as well.
“You will come tomorrow,” said the man.
“Yes,” I said. I had been well-trained to answer such non-questions.
“Yes?” said the man, clearly surprised. “We had feared you would not want to join us. We are going to scavenge, and it is not safe here. But it is decided then.” He said with a smile. “Come,” he said.
The pair, the old one, and the young, led me into a former ball room, where the fire blazed on bare metal, ringed-in by heavy anchor chain, links big enough to put your foot through.
The sea gypsies lined the walls, kneeling in rows four-deep all the way around, six-deep in some places. A young boy held the ubiquitous hat out to me, and I bowed for him to put it on me. It was tight, but it made me feel slightly less awkward.
[Author's note: Research Banguigui customs, esp interactions with western visitors.]
The chiseled young man took me to the top of the tower, supporting me much of the way as I protested on behalf of my atrophied legs. But he was persistent, and when we arrived in a spire peak, I saw why. Over a low rail, I could see the whole town sprawling around the base of the tower. We were afloat in the ocean on an artificial island cobbled together of flotsam.
After the ceremonies, I joined Noe in his family's cabin built atop a catamaran. Through the walls, I heard the rattle of chains clacking across metal. At first, there were only one or two, then a few more, and soon, the individual clatters became one gurgling noise. Noe and his family were wrapping and placing seemingly random household items—a brass vase, a box of tea—into a large metal box. When a woman, presumably Noe's wife, saw me, she protested, saying something in the strange Spanish patois. It was clear she didn't want me there, and I bowed my head to step back outside onto the boardwalk, where the clatter was a waterfall roar.
Seeing the family struck a chord in me. I never did have a family of my own, not a real one. But I remember being part of several. Behavior problems sent me from home to home throughout my teen years, and I never did participate in anything like helping my parents pack a trunk of valuables. There was something about that. I don’t know. It got to me.
Disgusted with myself, I wiped the tearwelling from my eyelids.
“Siento, siento,” said Noe with his hands in the air before him. He shut the rickety honeycomb plastic door behind him.
Noe put a hand on my shoulder, and though it was gentle, I flinched. Noe grimaced at my timidity and almost shook his head. Then, his demeanor shifted abruptly. 
“Durme por Jiho la noche,” he said, laughingly.
#
Jiho turned out to be a tiny kayak suspended above the entrance to the town hall, and accessible only after Noe set up a one-post ladder with a few rungs missing. “Honor grande,” Noe had said, but I suspected the reason they had me sleep with Jiho was because she was visible to virtually every shack and hut in what passed for a central square.
The shiny red kayak was a cocoon, swaying at about twice the rate of the village itself, the crimson glow of the Hall’s stadium lighting filtered through Jiho’s hull cast a shadow across my eyes in the shape of the craft’s name. When the light shut out with a klang! I was alone, floating in the swaying darkness, swaddled in my clothes alone as I had slept every night for the last fourteen years. I got to sleep well enough, but I awoke before dawn with dreams of jelly sea creatures storming the village, prying me bodily from a red locker that must’ve been dream-Jiho.
Noe found me staring down the dock, and put his hand on my shoulder in a gesture that was becoming almost comfortable. I had stopped flinching at any rate.
He pointed to the end of the dock and I saw, like the specks of distant birds in flight, a fleet of what must've been jet skis."Vamos!" he shouted with a krinklefaced chuckle. He shooed me down the dock. "Vamos, vamos, vamos!" he repeated all the while as I boarded the bobbing jet ski. I cranked the accelerator fast, too fast. It tossed me in the water and I flailed and choked and saw a splash next to me that I mistook for an explosion. By the time I realized it was Noe, jumped in to save me, I was in tears with laughter. Noe shook his wet hair, splashing me like a freshly bathed dog. It was my first laugh since I lost my fingernails, and the first genuine, untempered joy since I don't remember.
#
We worked til dusk, skiing from patch to patch, picking pieces from submerged masses of flotsam. When we were about to head back--or, at least, I'd hoped we were--a sound, a shout from the lead skier. A wave of the arm propagated from person to person, back through the dispersed villagers, and like a pack of wild dogs, they fell into one double line.
In the distance, I saw a peak, like a little mountain on the ocean. As the line of jet skis forded the wide ocean into orange pools of sunset, the dark shape grew. It was an island.
No, as we drew closer, I saw it was no island at all. It was a floating yacht, upended so the bow jutted from the water vertically. Around it like seaweed surrounding floating driftwood, was a clot of…of…things. All sorts of things, but mostly plastic zip ties. I had to laugh. It was a bitter laugh. I had spent so many years shackled about the wrists and ankles with such ties. Noe's wife gave me a quick quixotic glance and I stopped.
Following the suit of the villagers, I slowed my jet ski as we plowed through the floating zip tie jungle, and slowly scooted up onto the edge of a more substantial clot made primarily of milk jugs, hardened over in calcarious concretions. The jugs cracked under the hulls of the jet skis, but soon our vehicles were moored as solidly as if we were beached in lime sand.
I looked around, and was reassured that a couple of the villagers were circling out at sea, keeping watch, and carefully, I dismounted the jet ski and tip-toed onto an island of mineralized plastic. The yacht's hull jutted from the concretion of trash, and I used it for balance. As the villagers rounded this artificial peak, they picked among the milk jugs, finding a piece of glass here, a rusted key chain there. One time, a child yelped with joy at pulling a thick silver chain from between the milk jug boulders. As we crossed around the bottom of the boat, a great squawking arose. We had disturbed a bird colony.
The villagers waved their arms, as if imitating the birds, and the birds mocked back, adding to the taunt biting beaks. But the villagers persisted, methodically gathering eggs from guano-covered nests. The eggs were passed back one pair of hands to another, in a train, that included me, and concluded in a pile near the beached jet skis. I passed the eggs along. They came quickly as I could pass. In the brief moment between passes, I tried to fetch a turtle scute that was wedged between the calcified milk jugs, only to find that I was holding up the line. It was the first scornful look I had earned since my time in the village, but it made me smile because I realized I had received not a single rebuke--save for the one from Noe's wife, but that may have been something else--since I had been thrown off the sea train.
At last, my desire got hold of me and I bent down to pick the scute out during a momentary pause in the egg train. It was jammed tight, and I had to stick almost my whole hand, more than halfway up the palm to get a pair of fingers forked awkwardly around its sharp end, like clumsy pincers. I wiggled it back and forth and back and forth for what seemed like a thousand wiggles before it cut me and I yanked back my hand with a yelp. In that moment, I looked up and saw that though I’d blocked the narrow ledge the egg train wound over, the villagers had not been slowed at all by my selfishness. The one in front of me pitched it over my head, higher now that I stood, and the one behind me, a young girl caught it in both her arms before swinging it around to the next villager and snapping round to catch another

BOOK FOUR: ROGUES

Chapter 00: Tin Can

Author's Note:  Robin Wagner backstory End of note. 


Robin Wagner:  “The docking rig shuddered and bent, six hundred meters of composite and refined titanium. I grabbed onto the hull and instinctively covered my face, but the lack of sound undercut my instincts and I turned to look again. It was a slow motion collapse brought on by a gas barge. If that barge didn't live up to its specs, there would be serious problems-the explosion would probably damage my own ship beyond repair. And with me there clinging to the outside like a beetle on a watermelon, I might have been be smeared across the hull.”

“There was a loud ping! and I flinched,” said Robin. “Popped rivets could start raining down any second. I had to get inside but I was frozen in terror and awe. I’d seen mechanical failures before, of course—what a sterile term that was—but I’d never seen a failure so large and, crucially, none that I was directly responsible for.”

“By the time I got into the airlock, the pinging of rivets were coming in waves. The silence of space was pierced when the vibrations carried through the hull, through my suit and bones.”

—

“When it was all over, I was thankful nobody had been hurt or killed. I myself sustained the only mild injury, slicing my thumb open trying to undo my suit quickly and sloppily. I felt terrible for putting the six workers' lives at risk, and I prepared to tender my resignation.”

“‘Resignation?’” my boss laughed, “No, no, no. We have a big project for you.”

“It was the last thing I expected.”

“And here I am.”

—


Robin’s mouth was thin-lipped and wry, with light laugh lines and the same slightly cracked lips of all of us who worked and lived in the water-rationed desert outposts of the outer solar system. Her frame was small but I could imagine wiry muscles under the loose yellow folds of her space suit. Her helmet-mussed hair danced as she unsuited. 





You don't belong here!

Well, fine time to tell me!

Author's Note: What’s the name of the ship? How are names decided? The crew proposes and the captain decides, or the captain proposes and the crew decides? Coin flip to determine which? What’s a zero g coin toss look like? A coin catch? Do they have coins? End of note.



“So, how are we going to name the ship?” I asked. 

“It already has a name,” said Moos bluntly. “It’s the Li Guoqiang.”

“Who’s Li Guogiang?” 

“Famous test pilot.”

“That’s not a bad name.”

“Yeah. But we can give her a nickname, can’t we?”

“Like what?”

“I don’t know, like…”

“Okay, fine,” said Moos, grabbing a helmet from the nearest locker, “We’ll draw suggestions out of a hat. Who’s got some paper?”

A quick search around the cabin produced a mostly blank page from a magazine, which Robin ripped into neat little rectangles using the edge of the table. 



Moos pulled the slips out of the helmet, reading them as he went: “Desdamona. Sky Kettle? Brew. Pot. Really? Peaquod. Hmph.” He sighed, “The fucking capital of Zimbabwe. Yeah, we’re not using any of these.”

“ Avuncular Ghost Machine.”

I looked at the one that called the capital of Zimbabwe. It was my half-joking suggestion: the Balanguingui.



“Any other bright ideas?”

“I thought ‘the Fucking Capital of Zimbabwe’ had a ring to it,” said Robin.

I whispered to Robin, “Not much of a captain, is he?”



“He’s a very good captain, actually. But he didn’t want this assignment.”

“Who can blame him?”

“Yeah. But you’re right, he’s acting like a child.” 


Throughout the rest of the journey out of the solar system, ‘TFCOZ” became our nickname for the ship pronounced “Tough-Cause”. 

Author's Note: Look up Chinese ship naming conventions maritime traditions and the name for Chinese cosmonauts End of note.



Author's Note:  They’re going to have to figure out how to “push” the Jovian nervous system on the exploratory ship… End of note.




Author's Note:  As the Jovians leave Jupiter’s magnetosphere, they “slow down” all of their vital signs slump. It turns out that they’re going to die because they need the Jovian magnetosphere “pushing” their nervous system. End of note.



Author's Note:   Robin & Luce solve the Jovian nervous system problem by removing one or two sections of magnets shielding from the quark barrage housing nearest the Jovian dorms. End of note.

“So, what you’re saying to me is, the Jovians aren’t going to survive this trip “
“They’re not going to survive leaving the vicinity of Jupiter.”
“Then we’ll pull them.”
“Robin has an idea.”
“Robin?”
“We could set up a coil around the Jovian portion of the habitat, and wind it up to a few microteslas. It wouldn’t bee to big a power drain.”
“Stop right there. We’re not rebuilding the ship. The Jovians can stay home.”
“But…”
“That’s final.”
 

“I have another idea. If we remove a section of the shielding from the quarkmatter containment torus, it’ll expose a portion of the ship to the torus’s magnetic field. Cheap and easy fix.” 
“But dangerous?”
“Hell yes.”
“Let’s do it.”

Turned out there wasn’t a panel aligned with the right section of the ship. The nearest one would also expose the mess hall entrance hallway to the magnetic field, so we went to all forty-four members of the crew, except for Captain Moos and explained the situation. It’s amazing that, even though they didn’t know the Jovians, as soon as you establish an us-vs-them team dynamic, just about every agreed. It felt good to do the right thing in spite of company foot shuffling. 

We suited up and went out. 
“How strong is the magnetic field surrounding the containment field?”
“Actually, the magnetic field is the containment field. I don’t know the specs.”
“Didn’t you design this ship?”
“Well, I designed the frame.”
“But not the engine?”
“Well, the frame and the hab module and the whole external shielding system. Sorry if that’s not good enough for you…”
“I mean… Nevermind. Sorry.”
“I’m kidding!” her tone said it all. “Look, the field is going to have a gradient. Close up, it’ll be really strong. But it dissipates very rapidly with distance. The shielding is has a core consisting of interleaved plates of alloys that serve to draw the magnetic field lines in tighter. We open it up, and the Jovians will be exposed to the gradient.”
“But how strong is it?”
“Not as strong as Jupiter, I assume. At least, not at the distance of the hab.”
“So, we shouldn’t have any metal objects on us when we take the lid off eh?”
“Well, not really. They could get hot.”
“How hot?”
“Not very hot if we hurry.”
I took a quick survey of the metal on the suit that I knew about. Elbow joints and knees, the connector at the neck. Nothing was touching my skin directly. There was fabric between. I supposed that was about like picking up a hot pan handle with a dry towel. Although, if I got at all sweaty on this little expedition, it could be a problem. I decided to heed Robin’s advice and hurry.


An announcement was made to the ship’s crew by the administrator. “We’re very sorry, but the Jovians will have to be removed.”

“But Robin fixed it! Shouted her lead engineer.”

“It’s been decided, and it’s not worth the safety risk. You will have to walk though a high magnetic field hallway every day.”

“We’re Jovians! We’re all Jovians!”

There was a great cheer. That was the first time I heard that word used to refer to humans, and I felt a tingle in my skin. Team loyalty was winning the day. 

“Now…” said the administrator. 

Moos chimed in, “This is my ship, and I say the Jovians stay.”

“Your ship!? It is Ramloco’s ship!”

The sullen administrator returned several hours later, told us they could stay. 


Seeing Jovians eating for the first time, Moos said, “That’s disgusting.” 

“As disgusting as psoriasis? As disgusting as rhinotexilmania? Drinking cow pus? All biology is disgusting,” retorted Robin. 

The ferry scooted in close, so that the turrets seemed to tower towards infinity, and encompass us like we were pulling into the harbor of a great metropolis. The woman next to me leaned over, apparently to get a better look at some detail. Usually, ferries were avoided and direct ship-to-ship docking was the norm, but because of the complex geometries of the hastily constructed interstellar voyager and the chunky bulk of the hastily converted cargo vessel, direct docking would be impossible.

From the outside, the ship’s bridge reminded me of a little wooden Orthodox chapel where I once helped negotiate the release of several Itelmen hostages. The ship’s skin panels were coal gray aluminum instead of weathered gray wood, but the placement seemed just as herky-jerky, piled in convoluted symmetries so the whole thing looked like a jumble of crystals grown in a laboratory.

At either end, there was a torus. One was about twice the size of the other, and was surmounted by half a dozen spherical components of various sizes. Brian said these were the quark and antimatter containment drives, and coolant systems.

  	“But where’s the shielding?” I asked. “Aren’t we going to get blasted by interstellar dust at the speeds we’re going?”

  	“Yep. And don’t forget about the radiation from the drive itself.”

  	“So, where’s the shielding?”

  	“Just wait.”

The ship’s drive was two toroids, one smaller one was for magnetically isolating quark matter, while the other was surmounted by an army of spherical liquid metal cooling units. The habitable portions of the ship were packed in between, along a long, fat central spine.

The cabins mounted on the main drive tube looked like a chihuahua trying to mount Marmaduke.

Normally also, new crews were introduced to each other in a semi-formal reception that had taken on something of the weight of tradition. Stories circulated about the opening parties for some of the more well known vessels. And some of the less well known ones had associated lurid details that circulated among consortium employees as rapidly as porn threads. But here we were boarding the ship that would be our home for at least the next several years, and I was surrounded by strangers. Only Brian was a familiar face, and he was seated three rows behind me.

  	“I’m not much for introductions,” said the woman who now leaned halfway over my lap and pressed her forehead against the glass.

  	“Me either,” I said.

  	She sat upright. “I’m Robin.”

  	“Luce Fagan. Nice to meet you. What do you do?”

  	“I’m the mission engineer,” she said.

  	“I’m the cook.”

  	She looked at me, quizzically.

  	“And the head linguist. No, really.”

  	“Impressed,” she said.

“This is the first constant acceleration ship built to carry humans,” said Brian. “Or Jovians, for that matter.”

  	“There have been probes though?”

  	“Little ones.”

  	He held up a hand like he was pitching a baseball.

  	“That’s how they explored Centauri?”

  	He nodded, “And Tau Ceti and Groombridge 34A and Kapteyn’s Star, and Barnard’s. So, it’s not like it’s completely untested technology,” he said as if to reassure. But his tone wasn’t reassuring.

  	“It’ll be nice to have normal gravity though,” I said.

  	He nodded again.

A tiny chunk of quark matter sat at the heart of the drive, and from this a tiny amount of antimatter was produced. And from this, an enormous amount of thrust. Or so Brian had explained.

Gravity came on abruptly as the drive kicked into action for the first time. Once triggered, the reaction would be self-sustaining, and it would require a great amount of energy to shut down. Thus, it was determined that testing it would be beyond the means of the development team, and what we were experiencing now was, in effect the first test.

  	It’s not like it’s untested technology, Brian’s words came back to me.

  	I dug my heels into the seat’s stirrups.

  	My face was pelted with the tiny grains that always managed to find their way free from the ubiquitous mine tailings, suddenly finding themselves in possession of apparent weight as the ship accelerated up to the 1g point.

  	This wasn’t unusual. I’d felt it on the interplanetary as it was leaving Earth’s L5. What was unusual was knowing this acceleration would last for years, that for all intents and purposes I would weigh what I weighed on Earth. Minus the extra pounds. I was looking forward to it. But my muscles twitched as if nervous at the idea of bearing my body’s weight once again.

The ship was shoddily put together, but shiny as hell.

“The strange matter drive could be used as a weapon…”
“How?”
“Well…”

Author's Note: How could strange matter be dangerous? Under special circumstances, it "eats" other matter. In order for this to happen, the strange matter has to be more stable than the matter it meets and not repel it. If those conditions are met, the other matter will "want" to convert to strange matter, and contact between the two will get things going. The result would be an ever-growing ball of strange matter, burning through matter like a fireball. End of note.



Author's Note: For such a disaster scenario to occur on Earth, strange matter would have to remain for more than a fraction of a second at earthly pressures, and we don't know if it can do that. It would also have to be negatively charged.

 



Author's Note: In fact, potential strange matter would probably be positively charged, says Farhi. And since the matter on our planet (including us) has positively charged atomic nuclei, it would repel strange matter. "If you had a little lump on the table, it would just sit there,” End of note.



Author's Note: The scenario would change if strange matter were negatively charged, and a ball of it was madly rolling around on Earth. "You would probably know it because it would be growing and consuming everything at its border, End of note.






“Captain Moose,” I started.

  	“It’s pronounced Moze, and I’m not your captain. I’m just  a coordinator.”

  	“Yes sir,” I said. “But I just wondered…once they spray on the shielding, how are we going to get out of this snowball?”

  	“Take your seats kids,” said Moos.

  	I strapped in, and Robin strapped in next to me.

  	I tried one last time, “Where’s the port?”

  	Moos pointed out the window to the long drinking straw of a conduit I’d noticed on docking. That was barely big enough for a human. A Jovian would have to squeeze through it like a plunger in a syringe.

  	A dollop of white spattered the window.

  	“Gross,” said Robin.

  	I just stared.

  	It was snowing flakes the size of my head at first, landing with a splat. Then it was flakes the size of a full grown man, then the size of a Jovian, and then they were stacked too deep to see out anymore.

  	For over an hour, the splattering got louder and louder, sounding like a truck driving through winter slush. As the coating got deeper and deeper, the sounds became more and more watery, and the shaking dampened.

  	“I wonder how we’re supposed to see out?” I mused, but it seemed Robin was asleep.

  	Then she shot awake.

  	“Sorry,” she sputtered, jerking her head back and forth, “What?”

  	“Settle down,” I said, “I was just talking to myself.”

  	“It’s glass gel in the front.”

  	“What?”

  	“We’re in the back of the ship; this goop is radiation shielding. In the front, it’ll be micrometeor shielding, which is mostly transparent.”

  	“Oh, I thought you were asleep.”

  	“I don’t miss anything,” she yawned.

  	“So, this is to protect us from the engines, but the front will have something clear?”

  	“Yeah, it’s spray-on too.”

  	“And you know this how?”

  	“I designed it.”

  	“Impressed.”

  	“It’s a gradient, the denser water-ice based stuff in the back, doped with borax and beryllium compounds to bock the radiation. In the front, the lighter impact-resistant stuff glass gels. The only problem is, with ablation, the front will become less and less transparent again. At least, that’s our best guess. Nobody knows how dense the interstellar medium is in this direction. So, probably before we return, or as soon as we get to our destination, we’ll need to do a bit of polishing. Maybe a lot.”

  	“Bored,” I said.

  	She looked at me, taken aback.

  	“Just kidding!”        	

Eventually, we were allowed out of our seats again. Robin had nodded off on my shoulder, and I didn’t want to disturb her, so I stayed in place while everybody else went about exploring the spaces that would be all of our home for the next six years at least.

  	I was just putting my hand on Robin’s forearm to rouse her when Brian walked by.

  	“God, she looks just like your sister,” he said.

  	“No she doesn’t,” I said, doubting myself. They did both have a nice smile and intelligent eyes.

He just raised his eyebrows.

 

The radiation shielding kept raining down, raising to a roar for a time, then slowly tapering off to sounds like underwater gurgling while the violent shudders calmed to a soft vibration. It felt like there was a resonance to the vibration that led to a slight rocking.

From the back ports, it was like looking into a clear blue glacier, darkness closing completely within a few feet of the glass. In the center and front of the ship, the fluffy cottonlike ablation shielding obscured the ports entirely. I had to trust Robin that the very front of the ablation shielding would eventually compress into a clear lens of window before frosting again as the ship encountered the expected microdusts of the interstellar medium.

 

Ablation shielding was sprayed on to the front of the craft, while water-ice based radiation shielding is sprayed onto the rear. As time went on, the sound was more and more like being underwater, and the shaking of the ship’s frame dropped off until it felt steady as rock.

Over the trip, the ice would compact towards the front, becoming more transparent for a better view, and this should continue throughout the flight. By the we they reached the rogue planet, we should be able to see out clearly. The ice in the rear was opaque, doped with compounds of borax and beryllium for radiation absorption.

Her description conformed to the holoprojection Moos kept on his desk. According this, from the outside, the ship was something like a squat dogbone or bowling pin. The small end was translucent white and the big end was translucent blue. The spires of the ship were barely visible through the icy surface.

 

SETTLING IN

  	It took several months



Author's Note: ? End of note.



to reach the edge of the solar system, and by then, we were only accelerating at .7g, but life aboard the ship was starting to feel like life aboard a ship; there were starting to be things to do. Monitoring tiny meteorite collisions occupied a good amount of Moos and Robin’s time. I helped the Jovians test their space suits.

  	No Jovian had ever worn a space suit before, and they took a bit of cajoling in order to get them comfortable with the idea. Apparently, the hatch was designed to be traversed in shipboard scrubs, and we were meant to change into space suits in a small outer bubble of a hatch when we got to the end of the claustrophobic tube.

  	As such, the pressure had to be suitable for both species—with a punishing definition of “suitable”.

  	My ears felt like they were being stabbed by the sulphur-stinking air. The Jovians complained that their eyes stung if they kept them open, but they had a tendency to get turned around if they closed them. Eventually, we worked out a system by which I would guide them forward by constant taps on their domes.

  

Author's Note: Robin and Luce spend more and more time together. End of note.

Author’s Note: Moos decides to embrace the joking about his name, like pluralizing it as Meese. He takes to calling the crew his moslings. End of note.

Robin’s cabin was smaller than mine, sparse as well, but she had one thing I didn’t: pictures. 



They were all pictures of herself doing something; standing in front of engineering projects, mostly. One was her, I presume, in a space suit, standing on the surface of the moon, next to the now iconic tilted, bone-white sun-bleached Apollo flag. 



“All my accomplishments. I have to keep them around to remind myself.” 



“Hmmm. I don’t think much of my accomplishments. I guess I haven’t accomplished anything.” 



She didn’t move away when Luce stepped in closer. 



Their eyes were locked. She pressed closer. Luce wrapped his fingers around the upper buttons of her jacket. She sighed, and he pulled her in, then proceeded to unbutton the jacket, unconsciously mouth-breathing while her rib cage rose and fell in deep, breathy pulls of air. 



Author's Note: Author's Note:  falling in love… 



Prelude: Brian? Moos?



Moments out of time>>>Luce’s education on all things Robin>>>Robin’s story<<<Shared loneliness.



Surprise connections>>>something other than languages>>>Toronto<<<forgotten memories



Robin likes Marem.



Darknesses.



He talks about Sakha; she asks about landforms, and explains geology>>>geology metaphors?



Geology of sakha 

 End of note. End of note.



“Alright, Moose,” I said. 
Was it funny to call the captain “Moose” or did I just think it made the crew like me—or just Robin? 


Author's Note: Robin is an addict too. How do they learn about each others’ addiction? End of note.



Author's Note: They do stims together, and she shows him something new. End of note.

“Try this,” she said, rolling up several of her stim patches and twisting them so they made a scant few drops of milky liquid on the nightstand. Then, she wiped it up with her finger and rubbed it around the inside of both nostrils.
She gripped her knees and tensed, singing deeper into the bed as she leaned slightly back with her eyes half closed. She breathed deeply, her shoulders rising and falling sensuously. Soon, she was rocking back and forth, rubbing her palms on her knees, fingers splayed, undulating her whole body, practically writhing. She opened her eyes and gave me a look that made me instantly horny. 
I hurried to follow suit, but had a hard time taking my eyes off the goosebumps forming on her skin as she rolled her shoulders and neck round and round. 
The stim liquid burned. It smelled like detergent. 
But the burn gave way to tingling. The tingling to warmth. And the warmth spread down, into my core. 
“The extra, can go down here,” she said, rubbing her moist fingers on her moist vulva. She beckoned me to join her.
I put an around her shoulders, a hand between her legs, and we enveloped each other in a dance to the rhythms of our whole physiologies. I felt like my nervous system was splayed out, strewn over the whole bed. I could feel every inch of fabric, every millimeter of her skin where it pressed against mine. All the little bumps of her areoles as they rested on my collarbone when she turned to straddle my lap. 

She told me that night of her history with Leo—Captain Moos.

I didn’t mind that she had an ex, of course. I did too, I could barely remember, those times lost so long before all of this—this experience of the last fourteen years. 

But that’s not what bothered me. Partly, it was the position of authority. A good commander…and a good man, would not let himself be appointed in charge of an ex. As unorthodox as this crew already was, that wasn’t a kind of lack of orthodoxy I was interested in serving under. But here Mos was, and here Robin was. And here was I. 


As soon as we were out of the solar system, Robin brought a concerned look to the bridge. 
“We’re experiencing bombardment by small particles. The rate has been up and down, but seems to be reducing with time.”
“You’re the expert on the interstellar medium. Tell me what’s going on,” said Moos.
“There have been few probes in this direction. This was thought to be one of the least dense areas for interstellar matter. We’ve certainly never detected any particulate matter here, or anywhere.” 
“But is it safe to go up to full speed?”
“I think we should wait.”
“How long?”
“I can’t say.”
“Give me a time frame. An hour? A week?”
“I mean, I really don’t know.”
“What do you mean you don’t know? How can you not have any clue? I mean, there are a limited number of possibilities, right?”
I bristled at how he was speaking to her, but she held steady. Not defiant, just impassive, contemplative. 
“Well, again, we just don’t know for sure.”
“List some possibilities for me.”
“Remains of a disintegrated comet. Asteroid collision debris. Maybe primordial chondrules I suppose…”
“You said it’s decreasing?”
“Yes, but let’s say it’s a micrometeoroid swarm—the remains of a comet, or asteroid debris, or something. It’s like a very thin ring around the sun, but like bigger ring systems—say, Saturn’s—it can have resonant structures. Thicker strands, and thinner. BOOK TWO: AMERICANA


Chapter 00: Homecoming

 

I sent the jet ski’s location in a message to the council’s handy. Hopefully, through the coup and all, they had retained the communal messaging system. They wouldn’t be too far away to send a couple scouts to pick it up.

The Midway Island Authority transferred me to a small cargo ship which was diverted just for this purpose. 

I was awoken one night by a sea train rushing by, terrifying in its scale and velocity. After being dropped off in Portland, I was picked up by a guy named Ry Taragan. 

Ry was described as an administrative assistant to the head of Ramloco. 

Apparently, the company had bought out my contract after the privatization of the United Nations. 

I got a few hours of rest before, I was told, I would be appearing at a party. 

I assumed it was in honor of my return, but it’s not. 






The Koryak appeared in my dreams the night after they set up an appointment for me to receive a new transdermal (teedee). 

“You're my ride?”

“Well, you're bright as a wall, aren't you?”

Crickets.

“Sorry, yeah, of course. Hop in.”

Author's Note: Ry picks him up for the party. He’s not ready, and Ry basically has to get him dressed. Ry walks him, almost literally dragging him by the wrist, to the car. It’s a hovercar, but it’s way nicer than the hovercars Luce remembers. End of note.



"Hi Mr. Fagan. I'm Ry, I work for the president's office of Ramolco, the oversight organization of the Midway Islands Restoration Partners. On behalf of the president, and our company, I apologize that we haven't had time to arrange a special reception in your honor. But your return coincides with a meeting of the partners and the international development working group, so we want to cordially invite you to the meeting, as well as the pre-meeting press conference."

I didn't know what to say, and I said so.

"The President will be there. The President. You should come."

 

I showed up an hour early, but Ry shouted "There you are!" from across the room. She pushed through the crowd and straightened my tie coarsely.

"Do you have any prepared remarks?"

"I didn't know..."

"That's fine. That's good, actually. All you have to do is stand there and look nice. You clean up really well, has anybody ever told you that?"

I rubbed my face. It felt gaunt, and I thanked him awkwardly, and told him he was too kind.

 

The president was short and round, short of body and of hair, round of body and of face. And she had to stand on a—well, a box, really—to stand above the bank of mics on the lectern.

 

“Ry,” I said, "do you want to get out of here?"

"You mean—? Oh—," he said, then pointed to his ring finger.

"Ah, I see. Sorry—"

"No worries, it's okay. Actually, the president is my wife."

I must have looked confused, because she said, "Sorry, not the President." He chuckled, "I meant Larnie Reyes, the president of Ramolco. Again, she sends her apologies that she couldn't make it. But she is a very busy person."

She grabbed him by the arm, and pointed at a crowd of reporters. A barrage of camera flashes and a round of applause rose and fell quickly. He tried to smile and wave, but it must've come off as half-hearted at best.

"Okay, we have to go now," said Rosemary.

"It's over?" I hadn't even noticed the President finishing his speech.

"These things are really quick most of the time. Haven't you noticed the pace around here? Follow me," she said.

 

She pushed her way through a shoulder-to-shoulder crowd. I was surprised to see her brush past the president—the President—and several men and women who, by their attire, must have been other heads of state.

 

"Luce, I want to introduce you to the Ambassador Dr. Siva Carter," said Ry.

She was a slight woman, but her handshake was strong.

"Pleased," she said, and walked off.

"Tough crowd, huh?" said Ry.

I raised an eyebrow and she laughed.

She pulled me over to a clot of people standing in a rough circle next to a tea service and veritable cityscape of liquor bottles.

 

“You should probably get showered,” said Ry. “There’s clothes in the closet.”

Luce doesn’t know how to pick out clothes, so the guy gives him some corduroys and a button up shirt, lamenting the lack of nice clothing. “If they wanted you to come to a party, they could have at least given you something nice to wear.”

“Who are you?”

“Oh, sorry. I’m Ry Taragan. Assistant to the executive assistant to Mrs. Reyes.”

“Mrs. Reyes.”

“The CEO…I’m with Ramloco.”

“Ram loco?”

 



“Ramloco. The Company. The Big Hand.”

Luce gave him an unintentional I've-been-away-for-a-long-time-look. 

“Oh, right. The Company wasn't exactly a big name when you went away.”

When I went away. That’s an overly delicate way to put it, thought Luce.

“So, when the UN got bought out—you remember that?”

Luce nodded. There was talk of partial privatization when he “went away”. Lots of speculation about what would happen to those NGOs that depended in part upon United Nations finding.

“Well, what were you in, LSF?”

“Linguists Without Borders, yeah.”

“Well, Ramloco, I mean—basically they snapped up—that is, they bought—all the crony—we, ah sorry—the ah—they—rehabbed a number of the UN’s dependent agencies.”

“LSF wasn't a depend—”

“Anyway,” Ry continued, “your contract was retained. Since you were MIA—as a courtesy. You know?”

“I get it.”

Ry nodded, with a look of self assured finality. 

“So, I'm an employee.”

“Oh, no! Well, not really. It's—it's, um.” Ry clicked his tongue. “Think of it this way… You've got a contract. It's you're old contract, exactly like your old contract except with an addenda with some extra benefits. I mean, you can opt in to some…benefits. At least, for now. You'll have to eventually decide.”

“What ‘benefits’?” 

“Really, it's all very good. You get to take your pension early and keep it up indefinitely.”

“Or?”

“Or. You can chose to terminate the contract at will, with no penalty.”

This part of Ry’s spiel seemed rehearsed. 

“No penalty except I lose my pension. The pension I earned.”

“Ah, well there's that. Since the NS—F whatever. They owed it to you. Look at your old contract—I have it here—”

Luce waved it off.

“Well, since Linguists Without Ff—Without Borders doesn't exist…” At least he learns, thought Luce. “Well, they owed you something. In the past tense. As I said, Ramloco is giving you the option. As a courtesy. Same old contract, pensions and all. Plus hazard pay. Back hazard pay!”

“Plus the addendum.”

“Oh yeah, but that's nothing.” Too casually dismissive. Rehearsed no doubt. “In fact,” as if an afterthought, “it's just like mine. Same standard contact all employees get. Except, right? You aren't even an employee exactly yet. So it’s kinda special for you, bud. Opt in. Opt out.”

It was starting to make some sense. “So, in opt in and I get my earned benefits, plus extra ‘benefits’, like…”

“Standard stiff. Hell, even interviewees have to sign this stuff. Noncompetition clause, no divulging of Company secrets,” he laughed brittlely, “which doesn't really matter to you since you have your pension. You won't be officially hired. Kind of a loophole. Technically an employee, but not holding any real position. For all intents and purposes, you'd be retired.”

“Mm hmmp. So, they could call me back if—”

Ry chuckled, “I don't think he’d want—”

“Who’s ‘he’?”

“Oh yeah, well, um…he—I think it's okay to…yeah. Um, Brian, um—you probably remember Brian Lum—”

I cut him off with a nod, then pushed by him toward the door. Brian Lumiere. Yeah, I remembered.







I opt out, I lose them. And I suppose 





Ry had talked him down, “At least have some free food and drinks before coming to a decision,” he had said, making a fancy champagne glass gesture and a nod and wink. 

“So, how was your quarters?” a stranger asked as Luce pulled at the crotch seem in his trousers.

“Terrible. Dirty. Smelled like horse urine.. But I got used to it,” said Luce, as Ry pulled him along.

“He meant the apartment,” Ry laughed.

“Who is he?”

“HR.”

“How does he know me?”

Ry laughed aloud. Luce thought it sounded condescending. But his demeanor immediately changed to upbeat matter-of-factness.  “Well, he should, he booked your quarters for you.”

They stopped at the top of a long flight of opulent stares above a gilt ballroom packed with new fashion austerely elegant suits and dresses. All eyes were on them.

“So, how's this for a homecoming?”

“Not what I expected.”

“Not this.”

They descended the steps to a torrent of applauds. 



Author's Note: Luce gets pulled aside by men with barely-concealed sidearms. They start asking him questions he doesn’t understand. Come to think of it, they don’t really seem to understand the questions either. End of note.



Author's Note: He's pulled aside by a secret agent asking what his connection is with  When Luce actually realizes he's talking about the Koryak, who they apparently found in the container, which landed on top of a deep sea mining unit—Carter offers to sit alongside as his lawyer, since she's got a degree in international law—Luce admits to having killed the guy. The agent clears the room, including Carter, and says nobody will lose sleep over this guy who killed his family, but they don't need an international incident on their hands, so he tells Luce never to talk about that again, and to find a way to convince Carter she didn't hear it. End of note.



"What's your connection with Igiklav Noooo-nut-nut-noo-noo-tan-kaaa—vaaaa— Nuu-tan-KA-VA-VO-vich?"

When he finally got it out, I said, "Nutankavavovich," though I couldn't figure out what ethnicity it was. I knew it was Russified something or other. Probably. Something from the Russian Far East, for sure. Igiklav Nutankavavovich. Sounds Chuvash maybe.

"He's a Russian national from Vladivostok. We think."

Then it dawned on me. No...

"What else do you know about him?" I asked.

"Well, your friend—or whoever he was—was found at the bottom of the Pacific. You said you were thrown off a sea train in a shipping container?"

"A red one," I said.

"Yeah, well. I'll check on the color. But this Igiklav guy was found at the bottom of the ocean in a shipping container full of shoes."

"That's the one," I said. I shuddered inside.

"Well, it damn near landed on top of an autominer. Ended up blocking its rounds, and when it radioed to Pacific Magnesium, they went down to investigate. They pulled him out last week, and we got called in." He paused, like he was waiting for something, then went on, "I saw him myself. The guy looked like he was made out of Greek yoghurt—sorry if you knew him..." He said, and he leaned in like he was looking for a reaction.

The Ambassador squeezed my arm.

"It was the Koryak, wasn't it? Yeah, that's who you're talking about. I'm surprised he looked like anything," I said.

"What do you—" he started, but I knew what he was going to say.

"I killed him. I smashed his head in with a—"

"Clear the room," he said to the air.

Another two agents, or whatever, came in and escorted Carter out, though she protested: "I'm his council—I demand..."

The door shut.

"What do you know about Mr. Igliklav?"

"Not much. I killed him. He deserved it."

"Nobody's going to shed a tear over the guy, trust me. He killed his family—wife, kids. Even killed his herd of reindeer, if you can believe it. Can you imagine killing twenty-something deer with a knife? Unbelievable."

"Honor, I suppose," I said.

"But you can't talk like that. I don't give a flying fuck what you did to that shitsack. But we don't need an international incident on our hands. So convince your friend the Ambassador—cute, isn't she? ...just give her a reason not to talk."

"I'll just retain her as council, I guess."

"That'll do. Anyway, don't ever talk about him. I mean, tell me what you know, and then forget you ever met him."

If only.

"I told you, I don't know anything about him—" I paused, but he kept looking at me expectantly. "Ok look, they brought him in after a hundred and fourteen twos and fives...um, sorry...I mean," I did the math in my head, "I was with the Sakhas for about two years, but I made nice with them, so they changed me to Russian supervision, but I talked to them too—I knew a lot of Russian jokes from my time in Moscow. I think they brought the Koryak in—no, I know they brought him in—because he didn't speak any language I spoke."

"Or maybe just because he doesn't take no shit.... Didn't. Take take any shit."

"Yeah, all of that," I said.

"What else can you tell me about him?"

"He's cruel—was cruel. I don't want to talk about him."

The agent nodded, and gave me a card with a mail account scribbled on it.

"Call me if you want to talk," he said, then escorted me out of the room.

 

Will I eventually call the agent who left the calling card? It was the kind of calling card that would literally call him agent when triggered….that's how I knew the he was serious.

I took a breath and breathed in the courage to put to a hand and croak, "Hi, I'm Luce. I'm a translator."

Or, at least, I had been. Made as much sense as anything else I might've said.

A man with wavy salt-and-pepper hair down to the small of his back put a bottle down and smiled, saying, "We know, very pleased to make your acquaintance."

He clasped my hand in both of his, and said, "We're honored."

We stared at each other for a moment, then he added, "I'm Marem. I'm a musician."

The whole group, and some bystanders erupted into laughter. Ry pulled me close and told me what the joke was. Apparently, Marc Emile—Marem—was a major pop star.

Marem took a few moments to make introductions, and Ry excused himself.

It turned out that all of us spoke Russian, although Marem had an accent so familiar that I couldn't quite place it at first—not quite French. Cajun, perhaps? I almost laughed when I realized. Quebeçois? It was such a familiar accent in English. Funny to hear it in Russian. I almost reached out and patted him on the shoulder. A gesture I’d seen the Yakuts do frequently, declaring ‘My countryman!’ But I wasn’t ready to reach out.

Another man, a scarecrow-looking guy with a shaved head who Marem introduced as the director of the St. Petersburg Museum of Contemporary Art, had a distinct Sakha accent.

"I imagine what you've been through, Mr. Fagan." I waved this off, but he continued, "Nothing I say could begin to express my condolences, but I feel compelled to apologize for the conduct of my countrymen. They too have been through a lot."

Again, I tried to wave this off, even as the perversity to this guy's statement sunk in. And he went on, "but if you'll beg my pardon," he said, "I don't understand what drew you there in the first place. Many of us," he raised his hand, "fled our own land years ago."

My mind was reeling. They've been through a lot? But this direct question caught me off guard. "I, I—well, I wanted to feel needed. I wanted to help. Those people were at each others' throats and I thought I could do some good. I thought...I don't know what I thought—I fell in love with the language—Yakut and Russian—" but my Russian was failing me, and I switched to English. "It seemed as though I could grab the combatants by the lapels, and give them the words they needed to negotiate their struggles."

A silence fell locally, a bubble of stillness in the midst of the gala.

Several in the group took the opportunity to swig their drinks, or to pour new ones. Marem put his hand on my shoulder, and his glass in my hand.

I took a sip. Vodka with cucumber. I took another sip, then closed my eyes. I could hear the Koryak whispering incomprehensible in my mind. Another sip, then I turned to Marem and asked, "So, what kind of music do you make?"

"Sing him the Moscow song by Jove," said the bald Sakha.

 

That brought some uncomfortable laughs from around the group. The Sakha excused himself, and took a couple of the other Russians with him.

I touched my glasses.

I looked out "Moscow song" but just brought up a bunch of uninteresting information. When I added "Marem" to the search—I assumed the spelling, accurately as it turned out—I was confronted with thousands of audio and video clips, lyrical analysis, and dozens of commentators laughing as they watched a live performance of Marem at a Moscow music festival singing a song called, in Russian, "Letter from Sakha".

Hello mother, hello father...I have gone to camp in Sakha...the food is good here, tastes like leather...hope they let me write this letter... It went on like that, absurd, to the howling laughter of Russian socialites and international media. The sound poured directly into my ear, the video overlain against the background of the party.

While I was viewing this, trying sort out the video people from the actual people at the party, the real live Marem kept talking, talking, talking, in that grating accent. About what, I don't know. I was nauseous.

"I have to go," I said, brushing Marem's hand off my arm.

Dizzy, I made my way to a restroom. There are no stalls, just freestanding toilets and sinks. I bent over the nearest one and dry-heaved.

"You don't want to throw up there," a woman's voice said, "that's a bidet."

I didn't care, couldn't care. I just leaned there, breathing cold, ironically fresh air from the porcelain basin. The video kept playing... Ivan's lost to...diarrhea...Sven's contracted the pneumonia...I'll pay my respects to their remains...If I manage just to choke down this bologna...

I threw the glasses across the tile floor, thought I heard a gasp, didn't care.

I thought I fell asleep, and awoke to a hand on my back.

"Is it morning?" I asked.

"No, no," said a voice sweetly. "You were only dozing a few minutes."

I inhaled the chlorine-clean bidet air and looked up, into the face of the Ambassador.

"Dr. Carter," I said. "I'm sorry you had to see me like this."

"Nonsense," she said. "How are you feeling?"

"Better, I guess."

"Good," she said. "Will you join me at the party again? There really are many people here who wish you well. We did our best to track down your friends and family, but I'm afraid we came up rather short. We're still trying to contact people you might know. You have been gone a very long time indeed."

I held my mouth, feeling my eyes wet at the corners.

"Now stop that," she said, "I've met a lot of very strong people, but nobody as strong as you."

I smiled and felt a tear drip onto my arm.

"You okay?" she said.

"Yeah," I nodded, actually feeling lighter than ever, happy even. Really happy.

"Ok," I said, "let's go."

 

Marem had a tattoo on his forearm that looked like some kind of pizza. 

The good Ambassador Dr. Siva Carter introduced me to a lot of American and South Asian diplomats, and generally made nice with everybody. I managed to get through the rest of the party alright, but I was relieved when it was over. 

A couple of times I heard one or another of the party-goers says "By Jove!" 

Author's Note: …which triggers a conversation in which Luce learns of the discovery of intelligent (or maybe-intelligent) life in Jupiter’s cloud tops. Since then, “Joviana” is quite the rage End of note.

To my consternation, it seemed like it was only a skin-deep fad. Few were actually knowledgable about or interested in Jovian culture. Red Spot keychains and Io tattoos were as far as it seemed to go. 












Author's Note: Somebody at the party tries to mansplain Sakha to Luce. He doesn’t need to hear it because he’s lived it, and he knows the ins and outs it better than they do. He’s also not in an emotional state to talk about it right then.  End of note.

Ambassador Carter looked like she was about to introduce me to a bearded hulk of a man in an all-black suit. But the man spoke first.

“By Jove, it’s Lucient Fagan.”

“Pleased to meet you,” I said, reaching out my hand.

“P

Comprehensive Analysis of Nathan McKnight’s Fiction Writing Style
Sentence Structure and Rhythm
	•	Varied Sentence Lengths: McKnight’s prose ranges from punchy one-liners to flowing complex sentences, creating a dynamic rhythm. In his flash fiction “Miss Poughkeepsie 1954,” he opens with a terse hook – “Miss Poughkeepsie 1954 was not a woman.” – immediately followed by a long, clause-packed explanation of what she is file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu. This contrast grabs attention and sets a quirky pace. Likewise, “Bent ’N’ Dent”uses short, abrupt sentences for comedic impact (e.g. “Hole punch, girl, septum. Gnuff said.”) intermingled with an occasional rambling aside, mimicking a breathless storyteller. On the other hand, McKnight proves capable of lush, extended sentences when the narrative calls for it. In “The Gilgamesh Golem,” the titular character’s soliloquy spans multiple lines without a full stop, as he reflects in an almost biblical cadence: “This may be the last story ever written. I write it to God, who would leave me alone on this Earth where all the nations have worn down to plains…” file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm. The rolling syntax here imbues a sense of ancient gravitas. Across his works, this flexibility in sentence length allows McKnight to modulate rhythm—snappy and staccato during witty banter or action, then stretching out in reflective or descriptive passages.
	•	Rhythmic Repetition: McKnight sometimes employs repetition of sentence structure or phrases to create a particular cadence or emphasize a point. In “Prick City Blues” (an early, unpolished novel draft), the protagonist’s full name “Josey Davis Coelho” repeats insistently in narration file-cfcku4cbrqtkadv9p6kqz2 file-cfcku4cbrqtkadv9p6kqz2. While partly a quirk of the rough draft, this repetition also drums a steady beat into the prose, giving it a stylized, almost hard-boiled rhythm in places. In polished stories, McKnight uses repetition more artfully. “The Gilgamesh Golem” features a historical panorama where each clause begins with “before” as it lists waves of ethnic groups (“before the southern blacks replaced the Jews, before the Hispanic migrants replaced the blacks, before the Arab refugees replaced the migrants, and before the Israelis replaced them…” file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm). This anaphoric structure creates a rhythmic sense of inevitability and cycle. Such patterns show McKnight’s ear for rhythm, whether he’s writing in a rough-hewn vernacular or a lyrical, incantatory mode.
	•	Grammatical Experimentation: Especially in first-person narratives, McKnight isn’t afraid to fragment grammar for effect. “Bent ’N’ Dent” deliberately breaks rules to sound like a raw blog entry – dropping subjects, using slangy contractions, and even inventing words. For example: “Accidentfully told her my dentist’s fax number. What can I say; I was probably drunk.” The made-up adverb “accidentfully” and the cheeky semicolon illustrate how he tailors grammar to character voice. Overall, McKnight’s sentence construction is fluid and adaptive: he adheres to clarity but will bend grammar and vary length to serve the story’s mood – be it comedic abruptness, conversational flow, or poetic meditation.

	•	Colloquial vs. Elevated Voice: McKnight’s diction swings between earthy colloquialism and elevated, scholarly language, depending on the piece.
