Comprehensive Analysis of Nathan McKnight’s Fiction Writing Style
Sentence Structure and Rhythm
	•	Varied Sentence Lengths: McKnight’s prose ranges from punchy one-liners to flowing complex sentences, creating a dynamic rhythm. In his flash fiction “Miss Poughkeepsie 1954,” he opens with a terse hook – “Miss Poughkeepsie 1954 was not a woman.” – immediately followed by a long, clause-packed explanation of what she is file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu. This contrast grabs attention and sets a quirky pace. Likewise, “Bent ’N’ Dent”uses short, abrupt sentences for comedic impact (e.g. “Hole punch, girl, septum. Gnuff said.”) intermingled with an occasional rambling aside, mimicking a breathless storyteller. On the other hand, McKnight proves capable of lush, extended sentences when the narrative calls for it. In “The Gilgamesh Golem,” the titular character’s soliloquy spans multiple lines without a full stop, as he reflects in an almost biblical cadence: “This may be the last story ever written. I write it to God, who would leave me alone on this Earth where all the nations have worn down to plains…” file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm. The rolling syntax here imbues a sense of ancient gravitas. Across his works, this flexibility in sentence length allows McKnight to modulate rhythm—snappy and staccato during witty banter or action, then stretching out in reflective or descriptive passages.
	•	Rhythmic Repetition: McKnight sometimes employs repetition of sentence structure or phrases to create a particular cadence or emphasize a point. In “Prick City Blues” (an early, unpolished novel draft), the protagonist’s full name “Josey Davis Coelho” repeats insistently in narration file-cfcku4cbrqtkadv9p6kqz2 file-cfcku4cbrqtkadv9p6kqz2. While partly a quirk of the rough draft, this repetition also drums a steady beat into the prose, giving it a stylized, almost hard-boiled rhythm in places. In polished stories, McKnight uses repetition more artfully. “The Gilgamesh Golem” features a historical panorama where each clause begins with “before” as it lists waves of ethnic groups (“before the southern blacks replaced the Jews, before the Hispanic migrants replaced the blacks, before the Arab refugees replaced the migrants, and before the Israelis replaced them…” file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm). This anaphoric structure creates a rhythmic sense of inevitability and cycle. Such patterns show McKnight’s ear for rhythm, whether he’s writing in a rough-hewn vernacular or a lyrical, incantatory mode.
	•	Grammatical Experimentation: Especially in first-person narratives, McKnight isn’t afraid to fragment grammar for effect. “Bent ’N’ Dent” deliberately breaks rules to sound like a raw blog entry – dropping subjects, using slangy contractions, and even inventing words. For example: “Accidentfully told her my dentist’s fax number. What can I say; I was probably drunk.” The made-up adverb “accidentfully” and the cheeky semicolon illustrate how he tailors grammar to character voice. In “Fingertips,” he links clauses with commas in a stream of sensation (e.g. “I flipped it around, the dry wrinkles like tea leaves.” file-4nnutszh4kdtkbcgwqnv1m), a technique that blurs the line between action and image to immerse the reader in the narrator’s experience. Overall, McKnight’s sentence construction is fluid and adaptive: he adheres to clarity but will bend grammar and vary length to serve the story’s mood – be it comedic abruptness, conversational flow, or poetic meditation.
Diction and Tone
	•	Colloquial vs. Elevated Voice: McKnight’s diction swings between earthy colloquialism and elevated, scholarly language, depending on the piece. Many of his first-person narrators speak in a conversational, slang-laden voice, lending authenticity and humor. In “Bent ’N’ Dent,” the narrator’s tone is irreverent and wildly informal from the first line – “You ain't gonna find love in a bloody nose.” file-n87j9uf4lquc2xfuwbi6jr. The use of “ain't,” dropped g’s, and playful misspellings like “lunatisk” for “lunatic” establish a rough-edged, punky voice. By contrast, McKnight can adopt a lofty or archaic tone in other works. “A Tealeaf from the Tangledays” opens with a mock-academic introduction rife with formal phrases and parenthetical asides: “I hope the reader will forgive this too-lengthy introduction… but in this researcher’s belief, it is important to understand the historical context wherever possible” file-aarbw2ymksuiseqjz9cb4t. Words like “ethos,” “providential,” and old-fashioned constructions give it a dusty scholarly air – only to ironically frame a very unpretentious scribbled account that follows. This ability to modulate tone means McKnight can be wry and modern in one story, yet archaic or lyrical in the next.
	•	Humor and Surrealism: A streak of dry humor and absurdity runs through much of McKnight’s diction. He often introduces outlandish concepts with a deadpan delivery, heightening their comedic effect. For instance, in “The Hellfire Pigeon,” the father character casually mentions fantastical inventions in a folksy drawl: “quads were too expensive back then, and there weren't no such things as ostrichpillars til I musta been, ohhh, twenty-fiveabouts” file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp. The matter-of-fact coinage “ostrichpillar” exemplifies McKnight’s surreal touches – a bizarre hybrid idea presented as if perfectly ordinary. Similarly, “Miss Poughkeepsie 1954” maintains a whimsically dry tone even as it describes a grotesque being: the narration notes she “braised a mean rack of lamb” and collected kitschy figurines, quaint details that comically juxtapose with the revelation that she’s a reanimated pug’s head on a machine file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu. McKnight’s word choice often winks at the reader; even in dark or serious stories, he may slip in playful descriptors or ironic understatements. This tonal balancing act—mixing humor with surreal content—gives his writing a distinctive voice that can shift from light to dark in an instant.
	•	Voice Modulation and Register Shifts: Within a single story, McKnight is adept at shifting registers between characters or narrative sections. “The Hellfire Pigeon,” for example, features a teen narrator with a plainspoken, contemporary voice and a father who speaks in an older rural idiom full of “ain’ts” and colloquialisms file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp. The son’s dialogue (“No way, Pops… I'm a city boy.”) is snappy and modern file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp, whereas the father’s storytelling is rambling and nostalgically tinged with dialect. This organic voice differentiation makes their exchanges realistic and even endearing. In “Nellibeth,” the dialogue between the young rancher narrator and the outsider Poula shifts subtly as trust grows – starting formal and a bit guarded, then becoming warmer and more teasing (note how the narrator drops in a casual “Hell, we’ve been synthies for years” once he realizes they share a secret file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi). McKnight’s diction thus mirrors character psychology: guarded and precise when characters are wary, versus relaxed slang or affectionate ribbing once they open up. Overall, his tonal range – from surreal humor to sincere earnestness – and his careful choice of words allow him to create distinct atmospheres in each story while still retaining a recognizably witty, intelligent voice beneath the surface.
Syntax Quirks and Punctuation Habits
	•	Parenthetical Asides and Em Dashes: One signature of McKnight’s style is the frequent use of parentheses and dashes to inject side comments or clarifications. This can be seen in his more experimental or humorous pieces. “Bent ’N’ Dent,” written in the form of a casual blog, contains asides marked off by dashes or asterisks that simulate a narrator thinking out loud. For example, after describing calling the girl “Peepers,” the narrator adds an aside: “Again, I'll mention that's not her real name, so they wouldn't have said that even if they were around…” file-n87j9uf4lquc2xfuwbi6jr. The aside, set off with an asterisk in the original, creates a conversational, tongue-in-cheek feel. Likewise, in “Miss Poughkeepsie 1954,” McKnight uses an em-dash to comedic effect in a sentence with multiple clauses: “Nor was she a man, nor–though she braised a mean rack of lamb…–nor was Miss Poughkeepsie 1954 any sort of human at all.” file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu. The em-dash encloses absurd qualifications, as if the narrator is briefly defending Miss P’s homemaking skills before landing the punchline that she’s not human. These parenthetical quirks give the narrative a layered voice – the main description plus a wry commentator on the side – and are a hallmark of McKnight’s playful narrative intrusions.
	•	Creative Typography and Dialect: McKnight sometimes alters standard punctuation or spelling to convey dialect and emphasis. In “Bent ’N’ Dent,” he writes colloquial contractions like “harder’n the hard way” file-n87j9uf4lquc2xfuwbi6jr (harder than) and playful misspellings (“Ozhio” for Ohio, “gesturizing” for gesturing) to reflect the narrator’s character. He’ll even use capitalization unconventionally for emphasis – e.g. describing a girl with a “tiny silver HEART in her eye” file-n87j9uf4lquc2xfuwbi6jr, where “heart” in caps draws attention to the literally heart-shaped sparkle. In “Hellfire Pigeon,” some dialogue is written with phonetic flair (we see “pa” for Pa, and colloquial grammar like “weren’t no such things as ostrichpillars” file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp) and on occasion nonstandard punctuation to capture an accent or hesitation (the text shows question marks where an apostrophe might be in “Naw Junior?that's what Pa called me…”, indicating a dialectal contraction file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp). These quirks make the voices leap off the page, allowing us to hear regional inflections and emotional emphasis without heavy dialect spelling. McKnight’s approach is generally light-handed – just a few strategic tweaks in spelling or punctuation to convey voice and avoid burdening readability.
	•	Use of Ellipses and Silence: When characters trail off or when McKnight wants to imply unspoken thoughts, he uses ellipses and broken sentences skillfully. In “Nellibeth,” Poula hesitates to reveal her purpose, speaking in halting phrases: “Do you know much about... I guess you'd call it... meattech?” file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi. The ellipses here capture her anxiety and the delicate way she broaches a taboo topic. They also heighten suspense for the reader, stretching the moment of revelation. McKnight’s punctuation thus often serves a psychological function. In tense or emotional moments, dashes and ellipses abound, mimicking the starts and stops of real speech under pressure. Conversely, in moments of high action or decisiveness, his sentences tend to be clean and end-stopped, delivering a sense of resolution. By paying attention to these subtle syntax choices – a dash to signal an interruption, a semicolon to join closely linked thoughts, a question mark mid-sentence to indicate confusion – we see how McKnight punctuates not just grammar, but feeling. His varied and sometimes unconventional punctuation is not showy for its own sake; it’s always tied to the voice of the narrator or the rhythm of the scene.
Use of Metaphor, Figurative Language, and Sensory Detail
	•	Vivid Metaphors and Similes: McKnight’s writing is packed with imaginative figurative language, often startling in its originality. He excels at drawing metaphors from unexpected sources to illuminate a character’s experience. In “Fingertips,” a vignette deliberately focused on non-visual description, the narrator uses a cascade of metaphors to convey his emotional state: after burning his hand on a melted object, he compares the task of picking it up to walking a tiny dog and the lingering smoke to a yapping Chihuahua, concluding with the haunting image of “the stench of eighteen years of yelling still filled my lungs.” file-4nnutszh4kdtkbcgwqnv1m. In these lines, the smell of smoke becomes a stand-in for the acrid remains of a long-fraught father-son relationship – a powerful metaphor that merges sensory detail with emotional trauma. McKnight often mixes the mundane with the poetic: in “Nellibeth,”he describes a simple flower tucked behind a girl’s ear as “a strange intruder against her pale-olive cheeks and coaly eyeliner” file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi. This personification of the daisy as an “intruder” not only paints a vivid visual contrast, but subtly suggests the character’s dual nature (a gentle touch in a rough appearance). Across his stories, from the fantastical to the everyday, such colorful similes enliven the prose and frequently carry thematic weight.
	•	Sensory Richness: A hallmark of McKnight’s style is multisensory detail. He doesn’t just tell you what a scene looks like; he engages smell, touch, taste, and sound. In “Prick City Blues,” the street market scene mingles sensations: “the wind mixed the scents from the market” on a warm autumn day file-cfcku4cbrqtkadv9p6kqz2, and when Josey eats a kidney pie, “its musty flavor ooz[es] out the corners of his mouth” file-cfcku4cbrqtkadv9p6kqz2. Such details ground the reader in the physical reality of the world. Even in brief flash pieces, McKnight finds room for sensory anchors. “Fingertips,” being an exercise in non-visual description, is especially tactile: we feel the warm air in the palm, dry wrinkles like tea leaves, the sting in the throat, the carpet under palms, the heat of a smoldering object file-4nnutszh4kdtkbcgwqnv1m file-4nnutszh4kdtkbcgwqnv1m. This layering of texture, temperature, and smell immerses us deeply in the narrator’s moment of crisis. McKnight’s metaphors are often sensory as well – note how in “The Gilgamesh Golem,” the narrator (a golem) describes the sun as “kilny,” as if the sky itself were a kiln firing his clay body and words file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm. By fusing the literal (a hot sun) with the metaphorical (the creative/destructive kiln), he evokes both heat and hope in a single phrase. This sensory and figurative richness not only paints a vivid picture, it often conveys characters’ internal states symbolically through external details.
	•	Lyricism and Poetic Influences: Especially in moments of introspection or mythic significance, McKnight’s language turns lyrical. He invokes figurative language that carries a poetic rhythm or resonance of myth. For example, in “The Gilgamesh Golem,” the golem narrator speaks in grand metaphors about time and elements: “the salt-laden tides of the last sea” smothering words, nations “worn down to plains,” and his clay limbs potentially baking into “useless branches” in the sun file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm. These metaphors draw on natural imagery (tides, clay, branches) and give the prose an epic, elegiac tone, befitting the story’s apocalyptic and ancient references. Even in satirical pieces, McKnight can wax poetic for effect. “Miss Poughkeepsie 1954” is mainly absurd, but contains the almost whimsical line “leaked new red polka dots” to describe blood seeping through the character’s dress file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu – a grisly image made quirky by metaphorical language that treats blood as a fashion pattern. Such moments of poetic diction elevate the prose above plain description, adding layers of meaning or beauty. They reveal McKnight’s literary influences (he nods to everything from classic sci-fi to Borges and mythology in his introductions file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm) and demonstrate an intent to not just tell a story, but to sometimes sing it. The result is storytelling that can be as heady and emotionally resonant as poetry when the occasion calls for it.
Pacing and Narrative Rhythm
	•	Controlled Pacing in Short Forms: McKnight’s flash fiction and vignettes showcase tight pacing with careful attention to how information unfolds. In these very short works, every sentence propels the story. For example, “Miss Poughkeepsie 1954” is under 300 words yet manages a complete narrative arc with a twist. The pacing here is brisk: the first sentence reveals a mystery (she’s not human), the next few sentences build absurd detail, and by the end, we quickly arrive at her ironic triumph (accepting a pageant sash despite her grotesque form) file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu. The story wastes no time, moving scene by scene almost like a joke delivery – setup, escalation, punchline. Similarly, “Fingertips” unfolds in real-time as a single tense incident. The narrative lingers on each micro-action (snatching, dropping, crawling, flushing) such that the reader experiences it moment-to-moment, stretching out what is probably only a minute or two of story time. This slow-motion pacing heightens suspense and allows the emotional weight to sink in by the final line. McKnight demonstrates a keen sense of when to pause and when to rush: he slows down for emotional beats or descriptive richness, and speeds up through trivial details or transitions.
	•	Scene Breaks and Transitions: In longer short stories, McKnight often divides the narrative into distinct scenes or sections, sometimes marked with symbols or abrupt jumps, which creates a rhythm of its own. “The Hellfire Pigeon” is explicitly structured in numbered scenes, with each scene break (indicated by * * *) often leaping in time or switching between a storytelling flashback and present action file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp. This episodic structure gives the story a lively pace, as if cutting between mini-chapters or even filmic cuts. It also allows him to withhold and reveal information strategically – for instance, Scene 1 ends on a cliffhanger (the father promising a secret) file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp, then Scene 2 jumps to the next day, delaying the secret’s payoff and keeping the reader hooked. In “Nellibeth,” a longer short story, McKnight uses a mid-story section break (#) to signal a transition from an outdoor conversation to a later moment at the ranch house. The effect is a gentle ellipsis in time; the reader fills in that the meeting ended and now we’re in aftermath. These breaks prevent the narrative from bogging down in needless connective tissue, ensuring the plot moves forward efficiently. McKnight’s scene construction tends to focus each segment on a clear purpose – a reveal, a confrontation, a character decision – which keeps pacing purposeful. Even when his stories wander (as in the shaggy-dog anecdotal style of “Bent ’N’ Dent”), there is a sense of momentum fueled by the narrator’s urgent, headlong storytelling.
	•	Emotional and Thematic Pacing: Beyond physical action, McKnight paces the emotional narrative – the rise and fall of tension, humor, or wonder – with deliberation. He often begins stories in medias res or with an intriguing hook (a sudden exclamation of “Hellfire!” file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp, or a bizarre statement like “You ain't gonna find love in a bloody nose.” file-n87j9uf4lquc2xfuwbi6jr) to grab the reader, then backtracks or elaborates. In “The Hellfire Pigeon,” after the startling start, the narrative alternates between the father’s leisurely reminiscence and the son’s immediate project with the jar, a rhythm that interweaves backstory and present stakes. This alternation creates a balanced tempo: reflective beats to establish lore, punctuated by forward-moving beats as the protagonist experiments with the “hellfire” device. In “The Gilgamesh Golem,” the pacing is more complex and daring. It opens with a contemplative monologue (slow, solemn pace), then shifts into a narrative about Paul and Holly that builds from domestic conflict to a sudden, surreal confrontation with a tyrannical landlord. The tonal pace shifts from normalcy to alarm rapidly in the landlord scene (one moment Paul and Holly plan a wedding, next their landlord claims Holly as his own in a dramatic twist file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm). McKnight handles this by increasing the tempo – dialogue volleys back and forth in quick succession during the confrontation, with short lines and interruptions file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm. Once the shock passes, the story slows again into aftermath and introspection. Such modulation ensures the reader feels the story’s highs and lows: fast pace when adrenaline and conflict spike, slower when absorbing meaning or atmosphere. In summary, McKnight’s narrative rhythm is finely tuned to the needs of each story, delivering plot and emotion at a pace that maximizes their impact.
Character Development and Dialogue
	•	Implicit Characterization: McKnight often reveals character depth indirectly, through subtle cues in dialogue and action rather than overt narration. In “Nellibeth,” for example, the narrator notes tiny details about Poula – the dirt on her hands, the hesitant “snurf” sound of her laugh, the way she plants flowers in neat rows file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi. These observations speak volumes: her mix of nervousness and resolve, an outsider trying to fit in. Rather than telling us “Poula was hiding something,” McKnight shows it: “I could tell Poula was hiding something. I knew that look… I’d practiced for hours trying to erase that same look from my own face.” file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi. Here the narrator’s recognition of Poula’s guarded expression implicitly tells us he has secrets too, bonding them in mirror-image. This kind of psychological signaling – a guarded look, a too-long pause in conversation, a fidgety gesture – recurs in McKnight’s work. In “Fingertips,”although only the narrator is on stage, his very movements (snatching something from his son’s hands, then later crawling “like…begging for forgiveness” on the floor file-4nnutszh4kdtkbcgwqnv1m) reveal the fraught history between them without a word of backstory. McKnight trusts readers to infer emotions like guilt, suspicion, or affection from how characters behave and speak, making the characterization feel organic and earned.
	•	Authentic Dialogue: One of McKnight’s strengths is writing dialogue that captures distinct voices and emotional undercurrents. His characters’ speech patterns vary naturally with age, background, and mood. In “The Hellfire Pigeon,” the dialogue between the young narrator and his father rings true to a family dynamic: the father’s long-winded storytelling and colloquialisms vs. the son’s eye-rolling interjections (“No way, Pops… I’m a city boy.” file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp). The son’s tone is affectionate but assertive, showing both respect and teenage individuation. In “Nellibeth,” the negotiation between the narrator and Poula over the ranch is laden with subtext. They speak politely at first, but the dialogue is full of little thrusts and parries – “You don’t much look like a rancher,” he says, testing her; “Well. I raise animals, sort of,” she replies elliptically file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi. As the truth comes out (she’s into synthetic meat tech), their lines become more open and humorous: “You’ve got to be kidding,” he laughs, then later even a flirtatious “we’ll see” with a wink file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi. McKnight captures these shifts in tone masterfully, showing the relationship thaw in real time. Another example: in “The Gilgamesh Golem,” when Paul confronts his landlord, his anger comes through in clipped, incredulous questions (“Just who in hell do you think you are?” file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm), whereas the landlord’s dialogue is eerily calm, formal and possessive (“She is mine… I loved her first.” file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm). The stark contrast in their speech underscores the power imbalance and surreal horror of the moment. Across stories, McKnight’s dialogue not only sounds believable for each character, it also carries subtext – power dynamics, cultural background, emotional history – in what is said and unsaid. Characters interrupt each other, trail off, or choose loaded words, all of which make them feel like real people on the page.
	•	Emotional Realism: Even amid fantastical plots, McKnight grounds characters in real emotions and believable reactions. His protagonists often experience conflicted feelings that are relayed through internal monologue or narrated observation in a way that readers find relatable. For instance, in “Fingertips,” the father’s internal voice is not explicitly quoted, but we feel his turmoil through narration: frustration (“I snatched the damn thing from his hands”), fear (“my heart was threatening to treacle out my bellybutton” is how the Bent ’N’ Dent narrator describes adrenaline file-n87j9uf4lquc2xfuwbi6jr), and regret (the final line linking the smoke to “eighteen years of yelling” file-4nnutszh4kdtkbcgwqnv1m). These metaphorical expressions of feeling ring true to complex emotions rather than simple statements like “I was sad” or “I was scared.” In “Nellibeth,” the narrator’s suspicion and hope are in quiet battle; he wants to like Poula but senses something amiss. McKnight conveys this with candor and nuance: “She didn't seem right, but she didn't seem that sort of wrong… Their shiftiness usually had a missionary quality… Hers was much more of a skittish shiftiness.” file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi. The careful parsing of why she feels different (not a typical corporate prospector) shows the narrator’s cautious, thoughtful nature. McKnight is consistently attentive to motivations and internal conflicts. Characters often carry guilt or pride from past events – e.g. Paul in “Gilgamesh Golem” quietly carries the guilt of having blinded a fellow boxer file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm – and these inform their choices without needing heavy exposition. This emotional realism ensures that however wild the scenario (a mechanical pageant queen, a sentient golem, a magical jar), the reader can connect with the people on the page. We recognize the hesitation, courage, desire, or remorse that McKnight’s characters privately wrestle with.
	•	Growth and Change: Over the course of a story, McKnight’s characters often undergo subtle transformations or reveal new facets of themselves, achieved without blunt declarations. In the span of “Nellibeth,” we witness a change in the narrator’s attitude from guarded skepticism to tentative optimism (even flirtation) as he learns Poula’s true intentions and finds them compatible with his values file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi. This shift is shown in his tone – from peppering her with test questions to joking about being “synthies” too – and in body language, not an explicit self-realization monologue. In “The Hellfire Pigeon,” while the story remains unfinished, it hints at the protagonist (Junior) gaining a new connection to family lore and maybe maturity through the adventure with the hellfire jar. He begins mocking his father’s rural ways, but his giddiness with the jar and engagement with Pa’s tale suggest an embrace of that heritage and magic. Similarly, “The Gilgamesh Golem” presents a dramatic change: Paul goes from an ambitious young man focused on marriage and career to a dispossessed, vengeful figure willing to resort to violence and subterfuge after his encounter with the landlord file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm. The story shows his breaking point and hints at further transformation (possibly involving the golem of the title). McKnight often leaves the ultimate outcomes slightly open or implied, but the journey of character psyche is clearly traced through reactions and decisions. In essence, McKnight’s approach to character development is show, don’t tell – we infer who the characters are and how they’ve changed from their dialogue, behavior, and subtle narrative commentary, making the experience of understanding them a participatory act for the reader.
Scene Construction and Transitions
	•	Grounded Settings: McKnight demonstrates a strong sense of place and scene-setting, often grounding even the strangest story in concrete reality. He tends to open scenes with tangible details that orient the reader. In “Prick City Blues,” the very first chapter drops us into Central Market at closing time: we see “long shadows cast by the autumn sun,” smell mingled scents, observe an old butcher’s booth still lit amid the closing stalls file-cfcku4cbrqtkadv9p6kqz2. This gives a cinematic immediacy and a baseline of realism. Likewise, “Nellibeth”opens essentially in medias res on two people planting flowers at a ranch, with rich sensory cues (loamy soil, afternoon light) and casual dialogue that implies the broader situation file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi. By emphasizing everyday textures – dirt on hands, an old trowel, an ice man stacking blocks in Prick City file-cfcku4cbrqtkadv9p6kqz2 – McKnight anchors the reader. Then, he can introduce speculative or dramatic elements against this believable backdrop. For instance, when Nellibeth veers into discussing high-tech “meattech” laboratories on the ranch, it doesn’t feel jarring because the ranch itself has been rendered so authentically that the tech talk comes across as just another facet of that world file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi. McKnight’s scenes often balance realistic environment details with one or two imaginative twists, thereby maintaining plausibility while engaging our sense of wonder.
	•	Productive Ambiguity: While scenes are descriptively grounded, McKnight frequently withholds full explanations, letting mystery linger. He might show us an intriguing object or event and delay explaining it, spurring reader curiosity. In “The Hellfire Pigeon,” the very first scene revolves around a “hellfire jar” that gives off sparks – a peculiar artifact introduced with almost no explanation file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp. Only through the father’s later story (in pieces across scenes) do we start to assemble its origin. This ambiguity keeps us invested, mirroring the protagonist’s own discovery process. Similarly, in “A Tealeaf from the Tangledays,” the elaborate scholarly introduction raises numerous enigmatic references (the Keeper Creche, Master Esthen, the Fifth Age) without immediate clarification file-aarbw2ymksuiseqjz9cb4t file-aarbw2ymksuiseqjz9cb4t. The actual “found” text on the tealeaf is just a tantalizing snippet of a student’s crude notes file-aarbw2ymksuiseqjz9cb4t, leaving the larger lore largely unexplained. Here, the ambiguity is part of the charm – the reader is left imagining the vast world suggested. McKnight knows how to leverage the unknown: he gives enough context to avoid confusion, but not so much as to spoil curiosity. Each scene reveals a piece of the puzzle (be it plot or world-building), encouraging readers to actively infer and anticipate what’s next.
	•	Emotional Resonance in Scene Climaxes: McKnight often ends scenes or story segments on an emotionally resonant or thought-provoking note, rather than simply a plot point. For example, a scene in “Gilgamesh Golem”ends with Paul’s humiliation and fury after the landlord’s decree; rather than neatly resolving, it cuts as Paul is escorted out, burning with regret at not fighting back file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm. This leaves the emotional tenor – outrage and helplessness – hanging in the air, propelling the reader into the next segment eager to see justice. In “Fingertips,” essentially one continuous scene, the climax is not the physical act of flushing the object but the emotional revelation that comes after (“the stench of eighteen years of yelling still filled my lungs” file-4nnutszh4kdtkbcgwqnv1m). Ending on that line reframes the scene from a simple cleanup of a mess into a moment of personal reckoning. McKnight structures scenes to foreground the characters’ emotional or thematic journey. Action often serves as a conduit to an inner turning point: e.g., the slap across the street that Josey witnesses at the end of a Prick City scene file-cfcku4cbrqtkadv9p6kqz2 isn’t just a random event, but likely a catalyst for him to intervene or reflect (it immediately grabs his attention). By concluding beats on such notes, McKnight ensures each scene transition carries forward not just plot mechanics but the emotional continuity of the story. The reader is always aware of what the stakes feel like for the characters, which makes each subsequent scene land with greater impact.
	•	Transition Techniques: When moving between scenes or POVs, McKnight often uses clever devices to maintain coherence. In multi-scene stories, he might echo a line or image from the end of one scene at the start of the next, or use a narrator’s reflection to bridge the gap. In “Hellfire Pigeon,” after a scene break, the new scene often answers a question raised in the previous one or shifts location but maintains a tonal link (Scene 2 opens with the aftermath “the day after I found the jar,” directly following Scene 1’s discovery file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp). In “Gilgamesh Golem,” the perspective shift from the golem’s monologue to the story of Paul is marked by a line (“The story begins in Jewish Harlem…” file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm), which serves as a narrative handoff. It’s almost like the golem narrator is cueing a flashback, smoothing what could be a jarring jump. McKnight also isn’t afraid of abrupt transitions if they serve the story – for example, he’ll drop a section break and let the reader catch up through context after the break. But he usually plants enough contextual clues that we quickly discern the new setting or time. This trust in the reader’s ability to follow yields a crisp storytelling style; scenes cut in and out without excess explanation, creating a feel not unlike a well-edited film. The result is that each scene stands distinct in mood and purpose, yet the overall narrative flows logically and satisfyingly through these controlled leaps.
Genre Blending and Subverting Expectations
	•	Mixing Genres: One of McKnight’s most notable strategies is his fearless blending of genres and tropes. Rather than sticking to a single category like “sci-fi” or “literary” fiction, his stories often straddle multiple genres at once, creating a unique tone. “The Hellfire Pigeon” reads like a slice of rural coming-of-age mashed with alternate history and steampunk fantasy – it has a boy and his Pa, fox hunts and school troubles, but also futuristic quads, cyborg-ostrich creatures, and an uncanny jar of “hellfire” that injects a touch of magic or science fiction file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp. This blend gives the story an unpredictable quality: the reader isn’t sure if they’re in a folktale, a sci-fi world, or an alt-history yarn, perhaps intentionally reflecting the narrator’s own straddling of old family traditions and modern aspirations. In “Nellibeth,” McKnight fuses a contemporary Western (a ranch setting with cowboy ethos) with near-future science fiction (synthetic meat labs, environmental tech) file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi. The genre mixing here underscores the theme of old meeting new – it’s literally about the future of ranching. Similarly, “The Gilgamesh Golem” is a rich blend of mythic fantasy, historical fiction, and political allegory. It starts with a mythical creature’s perspective, transitions into what feels like a period piece in a 20th-century city, and within that hides allegorical references to post-9/11 geopolitics and ancient legends (Gilgamesh, golems) file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm. By undermining genre conventions, McKnight keeps readers on their toes; each story creates its own rules.
	•	Undermining Reader Expectations: McKnight often sets up what seems like a familiar scenario or trope only to turn it on its head. The flash fiction “Miss Poughkeepsie 1954” is a prime example: it begins like it might be a nostalgic or quirky historical piece (the title evokes a beauty pageant in 1954), but it immediately dismantles that expectation by revealing the “beauty queen” is a grotesque automaton file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu. The narrative then plays out the pageant trope straight – Miss Poughkeepsie wins the contest – even though she’s a horror, thereby satirizing the very idea of beauty standards. This twist invites the reader to question their assumptions (we expect a “Miss So-and-so” to be a human woman, and a story set in 1954 to be realistic). In “A Tealeaf from the Tangledays,” McKnight primes us for an epic piece of lost lore with his scholarly, reverent introduction, only to have the ancient text turn out to be a brief, snarky note by an apprentice complaining about their teacher file-aarbw2ymksuiseqjz9cb4t. The grand buildup collapses into a punchline, humorously subverting our expectation of profound wisdom from the past. “Bent ’N’ Dent” toys with expectations of a love-at-first-sight punk romance – it starts with meeting a manic-pixie-dream-girl type (Peepers with the heart in her eye) – but swerves into chaotic horror-comedy as the narrator is chased across states by her deranged, “pig-mangling” father file-n87j9uf4lquc2xfuwbi6jr. Time and again, McKnight sets up a genre cliché or familiar plot arc only to veer into absurdity or a different genre altogether. This keeps his narratives feeling fresh and original, as the reader can never be quite sure what direction things will take. The undercutting of expectations often also carries thematic resonance – e.g. exposing a satire (as in Miss Poughkeepsie) or highlighting generational change (as in Hellfire’s twist on history). It’s a technique that entertains while prompting deeper reflection.
	•	Use of Irony and Satire: Many of these genre subversions carry a layer of irony or satire, indicating McKnight’s broader purpose in blending modes. By mixing high-fantasy lore with a petty student prank (Tangledays), he pokes fun at the self-serious tone of lore in fantasy fiction, suggesting that people in any era (or world) are still people – prone to humor, pettiness, and error. “Miss Poughkeepsie 1954” explicitly satirizes beauty pageants and ideals: the absurdity of a stitched-together creature winning highlights how arbitrary and superficial such contests are. The tone remains dry and amused even as the content is bizarre, which is a distinctly satirical stance file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu. In “Gilgamesh Golem,” there’s an ironic parallel drawn between ancient epic (Gilgamesh seeking immortality) and a modern mogul (ben Muhammad) seeking to possess someone else’s life; by blending myth with modern setting, McKnight possibly comments on the timelessness of power lust and the tragic repetition of history – a subtle form of social critique woven into genre blending. Even when not overtly political or satirical, his genre blends often carry an ironic contrast: a gritty realist style used to tell a fantastical event, or vice versa. This irony can create humor (in comedic pieces) or a sense of uncanniness (in serious pieces) that reinforces the story’s impact. Essentially, McKnight uses genre as a toolbox, picking elements from noir, sci-fi, fantasy, horror, and humor as needed, and he delights in defying the formulas of each, resulting in stories that surprise and often slyly comment on the genres themselves.

	•	Flexible Point of View: McKnight is versatile in his choice of narrative perspective. He writes convincingly in first person, close third person, and even experimental frames, choosing the POV that best serves the story’s purpose. Many of his shorter works are first-person, which he uses to deliver strong narrative voices: the frantic, confessional “Bent ’N’ Dent” narrator, the reflective father in “Fingertips,” the candid rancher in “Nellibeth.” First person allows him to unleash the character’s inner voice directly on the page, complete with humor, bias, and emotion. For instance, Bent ’N’ Dent reads like a diary or a friend recounting a wild tale, full of personality and tangents. In contrast, “Miss Poughkeepsie 1954” and “Prick City Blues” use third-person narration, which McKnight employs when he wants a slightly more objective or storybook tone. Miss Poughkeepsie’s fairy-tale absurdity is enhanced by a matter-of-fact third person narrator who almost sounds like a folkloric storyteller recounting local legend. Interestingly, McKnight is not afraid to shift perspectives within a single narrative either. “The Gilgamesh Golem” starts in first person (the golem’s voice speaking to God) file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm, then transitions to a third-person storyline about Paul and Holly, and presumably might shift back or connect to the golem later, effectively blending a framed narrative. This is a bold structural move that asks the reader to recalibrate their perspective – a risk that pays off by giving the story a mythic framing device around a more conventional plot. Such shifts demonstrate McKnight’s structural experimentation and confidence that his readers will follow him across unusual narrative formats.
	•	Nonlinear and Experimental Structures: While most of McKnight’s stories progress linearly, he isn’t bound to strict chronology or a single narrative mode. “A Tealeaf from the Tangledays” takes the form of a pseudo-scholarly article: it starts with an introduction (complete with an academic tone and context), then presents an ancient text excerpt, and ends abruptly after that fragment. The structure itself is a pastiche of research literature, which is a clever narrative experiment for a piece of fiction. It requires the reader to play along with the format to get the joke and the underlying story world. “Hellfire Pigeon”’s segmented scene structure is another mild experiment – labeling scenes and intercutting a story within a story. The Tangledays story includes “[SIC]” and “[ILLEGIBLE]” annotations in the transcribed leaf text file-aarbw2ymksuiseqjz9cb4t, mimicking how a historian would present a flawed manuscript. This adds realism to the fantasy and also an element of humor. In some of the provided texts, we even see McKnight including “Intro by ChatGPT” or “Afterword by ChatGPT” sections (clearly marked), which implies he’s experimented with AI collaboration or meta-textual commentary on his own stories file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu. This blending of real-world and fictional commentary is highly unconventional – effectively breaking the fourth wall of the narrative to discuss style and theme (as the ChatGPT afterwords do for Miss Poughkeepsie). While those might be later additions outside the story proper, their inclusion in the document shows a playful willingness to play with form, even to the point of analyzing his fiction within the fiction package. All these structural risks – multi-perspective storytelling, story-as-academic-paper, mixing commentary with narrative – exemplify an experimental streak in McKnight. He is clearly a writer who enjoys tinkering with narrative form and exploring how format can enhance story, theme, or humor. Importantly, even his experimental structures tend to serve the story’s intent (satire, immersion, etc.) and not just novelty for its own sake.
	•	Foreshadowing and Circularity: Another subtle structural strategy is McKnight’s use of foreshadowing and callbacks that give his stories cohesion. He will plant small details that later become significant, creating a satisfying structural unity. In “Nellibeth,” early mention of the land-stripping “sinkfarm scouts” and carbon repositories file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi sets up the reader to suspect Poula might be one – a red herring that makes the reveal of her true aim (meattech) more surprising, but also thematically ties into the story’s environmental concerns. In “Gilgamesh Golem,” the very name signals the fusion of ancient and modern that the structure delivers, and the text invites us to “look closely at the names” for wordplay file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm – indeed, the antagonist’s name “Israel ben Muhammad” foreshadows the story’s religious-political allegory, and his actions echo an age-old epic jealousy. McKnight sometimes closes a structural loop by having endings that allude back to beginnings. While we don’t have the full ending of Gilgamesh Golem, one can imagine it circling back to the golem’s narration, completing the frame. In shorter works, the final lines often resonate with the opening image or theme: Fingertips opens with anger and ends with a form of reconciliation (flushing the object but not the pain), bringing the emotional arc full circle; Miss Poughkeepsie starts by denying identity and ends by oddly fulfilling it (she’s not a woman, yet she is Miss Poughkeepsie). These structural echoes give even the wildest tales a sense of completion and purpose. McKnight’s structural inventiveness is thus paired with a storyteller’s instinct for setup and payoff, which keeps the reader oriented and rewarded even amid unconventional narratives.

The Gilgamesh Golem: A Parable 
by NathanMcKnight
Though I begin this story with the sincerest thought to record events as they actually happened, I owe an absolute responsibility to history to inform the reader-should there be a reader-that of the memories I carry, those that recall days before my creation are somewhat unclear. Furthermore, the haste that I must necessarily employ ensures certain inaccuracies in the form of summary. And if the end-times sun undoes the magic that made me or bakes my limbs into useless branches, you should know that it is the same kilny sun whose light I count on to envitrify my words into the soft clay before the salt-laden tides of the last sea smother them out. 

The story begins in Jewish Harlem, before the southern blacks replaced the Jews and before the Hispanic immigrants replaced the blacks…

* * *

Paul's mother was displeased in the extreme when she found out that her money was coming from boxing. She had stopped taking the blood money, as she called it, when word got around the neighborhood that Paul "The Maul" Stein had ended a fight by clocking one of the Italian boys and blinding him in one eye. Consequently, Paul and his fiancée had a modest savings. 

They had planned to get married in grand fashion, possibly even in their own semi-luxurious apartment whose neo-Egyptian façade was shaded during the hottest part of the afternoon by the shadow of the new Empire State building, where Holly worked as an assistant executive secretary. It was the nature of their respective professions that they spent most of the day apart. Their only contact was at dinnertime, after Holly had spent a long day in the office without a break and Paul was readying himself for the evening's fight. Sometimes, the famished couple would go back to Harlem where Yiddish and Italian and Irish voices filled the air with the restless spirits of the old countries, voices that complimented Mother Stein's cooking like the spices of the east. Holly would impress them with anecdotes of rich foreigners who always seemed to make extraordinary demands of the secretaries or, on lucky days, to bestow upon them ludicrously large tips in exchange for everyday kindness. 

It was on one such occasion that Paul first heard the name Israel ben Muhammad. Holly normally paid scant attention to changes of leadership in the company, but the buy-out by an Arabian oil baron precipitated an especially large shake-up among the employees. "The stars portend opportunity," Mrs. Stein told her son knowingly. Indeed, Holly ended up filling her own supervisor's newly-vacant position as lead executive secretary, handling the appointment books of ben Muhammad himself. 

She learned of her new boss’s real estate aspirations on the same day that the change in management for the East Central apartment buildings took effect. Notices were first posted to inform the residents on that very day. They were on all the walls, and in all the mailboxes. They were given by hand to every occupant, sometimes more than once. The postings shrouded the fine sheeny wallpaper with a quilt work of mottled parchment.

In order to keep the "criminal element" at bay-some anti-Arab graffitoism had taken place in the otherwise immaculate children's daytime care facility-all residents were asked to carry punch cards. In addition, for reasons that were poorly explained, rent would be upped for certain occupants. Paul and Holly would have to pay more than triple the normal due.

The old landlord's chair and desk were replaced with a velveteen paisley dos-à-dos, and a new door had been cut, presumably into the adjoining suite. Paul defiantly pounded on the door, though he knew he wasn't even supposed to be in this office-cum-foyer. "Hey Mac, that area is off limits now," one of the janitors had explained to Paul, whose punch card was already scuffed and bent from being tried in all the newly-locked doors that metamorphosed the building into the impregnable Egyptian tomb its lotus trumeaux had always bragged it was. The janitor had diffused Paul's evident rage when he punched his own card, as payback he said, for the five bucks he'd won off last week's fight. "I wouldn't mind if you gave that new landlord a good right hook anyways, Slugger." But here he was, pounding on the door instead of the landlord.

A scratchy electric voice, like those at the larger boxing arenas warned that unappointmented queries may result in fees or even termination of the lease, and Paul argued with it momentarily about the appropriateness of his visit until he slipped the note under the door. The rent envelope came on the 28th of every month, and this one had contained instructions on how to contact the landlord for a lease review. Why the lease needed reviewing was second among Paul's concerns, which were dominated by the draconian restrictions on his options for an appointment: "Anytime after 4pm on a business day before this month's rent is due." 

"Mr. ben Muhammad will see you now."

The suite was air-conditioned-a luxury even for such a fine apartment building. The secretary directed Paul around the corner to the landlord's relaxation chamber. The conversation did not go well. Paul spoke, facing away from the landlord, who lounged in a freestanding washbasin, smoking from a long meerschaum pipe whose smoke did a better job keeping away the flies than the peacock plume he switched them with. Ben Muhammad sat quietly until Paul had exhausted his lexis in a blubbering plea that touched on the wedding, elderly parents, and the potential for injuries in his line of work.

"Please have a seat in the foyer while I consider your case, Mr. Stein."

Paul did as he was asked to, but he found himself scratching the extravagant gold leaf work from one of the dos-à-dos's arms. The repetitive motion calmed him.

"You will be billed for defacing the furniture. " The secretary's voice itched over the loudspeaker. "This fiancée you mentioned; she lives with you here, does she? In that case, we will have to relocate one of you to the nearest vacant apartment until after the wedding. You will, of course continue to pay the increased rates. If you are unwilling to comply with the rules of this building, you are encouraged move into any of the other East Central buildings, some of which retain independent management. That will be all, Mr. Stein."  

"Excuse me?"

"One moment Mr. Stein…Mr. ben Mohammad says that he will be claiming your fiancée as well."

"What?"

"Mr. Stein," it was ben Muhammad's voice this time. "Because of the problems you've caused here today, your tenancy has been terminated. The lease will be transferred to the name of Miss Landis. She will stay here with me, where you may trust that she will be in good hands."

"Just who in hell do you think you are?"

"Sir, please try to understand. She is mine. Since before you were born, I've dwelt on that face. I realize you love her, but I loved her first. You see, when my father brought me to New York as a boy, the beauty of American women astounded me. But there was one in particular. Her name was Honey. The wife of Milt Landis, her face caused my heart to weep. It was the memory of that face which I followed back to your country. Now, I've seen that face again, and it is Holly, the daughter of Milt and Honey Landis. She will be my bride. Please leave the premises now. Do not attempt to reenter your apartment."

"That will be all Mr. Stein," concluded the secretary.

On the way out, Paul regretted not provoking the guards who stood by to see that he boarded the elevator to the lobby. As he stepped out the front door, a voice sounded from above.

"Hey, you're the sparrer. Pauler the Mauler, right?" An overalled man squatted on the top rung of a ladder, holding a pile of gold foil in one hand, and a jar of glue with a paintbrush jutting from it in the other. He spoke with a Scottish accent. "Do you live here?"

"Not anymore."

"Too bad. I suppose you don't like the management? Well, a lot of folks round here feel that way. I can't say as I share the opinion, though. If it weren't for Mr. Mohammed, I wouldn't have a job. My family and me flew all the way from Edinburgh, and Mr. ben Muhammad paid for the Zeppelin tickets. He says he's going to make these apartments into a utopia. I feel like I'm working for the pharaoh himself." 

Paul threw his body against the ladder, and picked up the little man by the collar. Several onlookers fled, but one of them-the janitor from upstairs-swung a fist at the air.

Paul bloodied the artist's nose and lips, dropped him and boxed his ears; he would have killed the man if he hadn't seen the Tommie-gun-wielding guards appear. As he left the chaotic scene, he looked over his shoulder and the janitor shouted out. "Way to go slugger," he said, only to be beaten and dragged off by a gang of security guards.

Another guard hollered, "Cut him off, he's heading across the street."

Paul and Holly were supposed to meet at the foot of the Empire State Building, but there was little chance ben Muhammad would allow that to happen, so instead he hopped a jittery trolley into Jewish Harlem. Ghetto faces lined with cracks stared at Paul, like ancient pottery sitting alongside a museum reproduction designed to imitate the beauty of newness. Mrs. Stein's tenement infested with age, from the ladies with pepper pot figures to the tall-hatted Hassidic men who discussed philosophy over chess. Even the Irish boys who played stickball out front seemed oddly wise for their age. Paul had grown up here, but he felt he had pampered away his street wisdom. He no longer belonged.

"What should I do, mom?"

"Stay here with me. Holly will know where to find you."

It took Paul a few days to realize that his mother was wrong. He had taken out his anger in the boxing ring. He told his mother of the Micks and Negroes he had beaten, no doubt winning his fans more than a few dollars. He didn't mention the Jewish boxer that would never again be able to bite into a fresh apple with his own teeth because of Paul's callused fists. One night, Paul went back to the apartment building dressed in his late father's ragged work clothes. Paul and Holly's apartment was on the seventh floor, and he could barely make out shapes moving in yellow light. He stared for nearly half an hour before he saw Holly looking out the window. He shouted up to her, but she didn't seem to hear.

"Paul the Maul! You don't look so good, slugger."

The janitor had a huge can of garbage that he dragged towards the alley. He said that ben Muhammad had allowed him to keep his job after he had promised not to talk to a single person while on duty. In the quiet of the alley, they talked about Holly's coming and going and the increase in modern conveniences, and the accompanying increase of security at the building. The whole place was air conditioned now, and the elevators were automated, but many of the tenants had been evicted to make room for newcomers who could afford the forbidding rent. Paul told the janitor that he was afraid ben Muhammad was holding his fiancée against her will. 

"There's a fellow might be able to help you. He's a rabbi."


Paul's mother was shocked. "Rabbi Samson's only a rabbi in title. The man is a lush. Don't you go near him." It turned out that Samson was a lascivious whoremonger who was rumored to masturbate at the talkie theaters. "Uncut Samson," they called him. He was, however, also a renowned mystic and that's what made up Paul's mind. Nobody doubted the Rabbi's powers. 

After a particularly bloody match, Paul delivered himself to a gas lit doorway that stood below street level only two blocks from his mother's apartment building. The door had a bronze plate inscribed with Hebrew letters, though with the streaked green corrosion and Paul's limited knowledge of Yiddish, he could only tell that it said something like "Welcome." 

Samson was a fat and greasy slob whose once-exquisite accommodations had been used beyond their capability, and now exuded a pungent fetor that seemed to waft out of holes in the carpeting. The rabbi glanced at Paul senior's clothing and said, "You can't afford my prices." Paul told him that there was plenty of money in the ring for anyone tough enough to claim it. Samson laughed at the implied threat, but waved him inside anyway. 

"I know of Israel ben Muhammad. He's obsessed with himself, like most of the world's better men. Your fiancée would be well off to stay with him rather than a low-born boxer from the ghetto." Samson left him alone long enough for him to reconsider his decision, but before Paul's mind could make sense of these awful circumstances, the rabbi emerged from behind a curtain-wall. "It is done. The girl will be yours. Now give me whatever money you have and go away." 

Paul didn't know what to expect, if anything, but he couldn't stand to waste time in actionless wondering, so he walked as fast as he could to the apartment building whose neo-Egyptian façade dripped silver rain like mercury in the bright moonlight. Holly was there, waiting in the alley. She was silent. Paul tried to talk to her, but she seemed not to know him. She didn't respond at all unless she was asked a direct question or given a command. 

"Are you okay?"

"Yes."

"What's happened to you?"

"I don't know."

He told Holly she would have to come with him, but she followed at a snail's pace, and when he carried her, he wasn't able to move much faster. 

The walk back to Harlem ended as the sun was rising over Mrs. Stein's apartment. Though he collapsed with exhaustion in his mother's spare bedroom, his mind was restless with angry confusion. Holly lay open-eyed next to him, and when Paul finally gave up the fight to keep his eyes closed, she accompanied him arm-in-arm through the foggy morning street. 

The rabbi's door appeared to be stout, but it only took one solid blow to unhinge it completely, allowing a cold draft to douse candles and to bear scrolls off tables. Uncut Samson was taken by surprise, nude, piggish, and shaking when Paul grabbed him by the arm, sinking strong fingers into the flab. A sucker punch to the face was stopped when Paul felt a paralyzing blow to his own spine. 

"Stay out of this. I'm going to kill him for ruining my bride." 

Paul turned on ben Muhammad and they began a dirty wrestling match. But, their battle was not yet to be.  The fleshy slap of each strike quieted to nothing while the apartment filled with thick incense smoke until both men collapsed in a desperate embrace. They awoke lashed together and suspended over a smokeless fire and immediately began to struggle against each other, against the ropes, and against the flame. 

"I will pay you," ben Muhammad yelled in between curses, "Holly, go get the money in my safe." Paul stopped slamming his skull against the other man's in time to see her run out the open door. It left both men relieved enough to stop struggling. 

“If you think I want Miss Landis’s body, you’re mistaken. Soon, I’ll have the body to take the women I wasn’t strong enough to take in

TITLE: Chewie
(c) 2005 by Nathan McKnight


Intro to "Chewie" by ChatGPT

Step into the grotto of Stig, a gnome with a peculiar devotion and an even stranger purpose. With vivid prose and humor dark as the underground, McKnight weaves a tale of faith, folly, and the mysteries of a world all his own.

Scene 1. THE GROTTO

Stig sat up in bed, shaking and ashamed. The scantily clad beard-nixies fled as his dream haze cleared. The room convulsed. The diorama he'd made from buttons and plastic dinosaurs fell, taking his felten cap with it. He yipped a feeble "Oh my!" then snatched up the cap, clutching it to his chest as the quake subsided.
Leaning back with a sigh, Stig picked up his old jimson pipe from the nightstand.
He would have to clean up after morning smoke, he thought, stroking his century-long beard and lighting up. He suckled the acrid smoke and sparkles infused his vision. Images of nixies danced in the harlequin tapestry behind his eyelids.
Then a lurch and shudder knocked the smoke out of him and the nixie visions fled again. 
"This is quite definitely out of sorts!" he protested, hopping out of bed with a scowl. 
He rubbed the sleep out of his eyes, troubled by a disturbing click-clickity-click echoing down from the grotto.
He padded through the soft corridor, trying to sidestep piles of moosh, but the shaking knocked him to the floor and he had to use his hands the whole way. By the time he got there, he was exhausting his repertoire of ancient gnomish curse words. When he finally made it to the end of the corridor, he wiped his hands on his overalls and yanked on the tail of the hairball dangling from the ceiling.
He pulled himself up, whispering the familiar oath: "Mistress Cindy, please forgive me my unclean dreams. For your slightest whim, I would gladly give my--" but he was cut off by yet a third tremor.
The hairy rope swung and Stig held tight. 
He climbed on, squishing his way through the tight passage in the ceiling. Fluid treacled into his eyes, and he held his breath, reaching through the squishy passage, wriggling himself upwards until he emerged, surfacing in the Reflecting Pool.
Sallow bile lapped at the base of the imposing Bezoar, his hand-woven monument to beloved Miss Cindy. Stig's nose twitched at its embarrassing unfinishedness, as it had been doing now for too long. 
The clickety-click echoed around the chamber.
But there was something else--Stig furrowed his eyebrows--an odd glint on the waves.
The Reflecting Pool had ever changed from blue to pink to green with the sweet rains that poured down. But this, this un-color glow was altogether different.
Her Greatness's grotto's lovely darkness needling with preternatural light, filtering down through the crenellated dome ceiling... He held up his hands and though his eyes were closed, he could clearly see the bones of his fingers.
Could it be? 
It was!
At long last, sign from Cindy!
"Hallelujah," he breathed, voice jumping to a shout, "Hallelujah! Praised be!"
He clutched his overalls and to his surprise, the medallion he kept tucked away in his pocket began to warm against his chest. His fingers prickled through the fabric as he grasped its dull edges. He'd prayed to the medallion nightly since he found it, but since the hairfalls had lately failed, he'd begun to doubt its power. 
"Dearest Miss Cindy," he said, kneeling.
A last click, cut him off, and the light snapped out.
Stig splashed to the quivering base of his beloved's Bezoar.
"O Miss Cindy! I have seen your magnificent light. Your revelation shall not go unheeded!"
"This is a great day in the Reflecting Pool," he whispered over the quiet drip-dripping.
Stig put his hand to his mouth and looked around, shooting glances all about the waves. Surely, the ethereal light had occasioned a hairfall as the cool sweet rains always had.
He ran his hands through the slippery liquid of the pool. Sure enough, there were some hairs. But just a few pitiful bits.
Stig pouted.
Where was the angel hair? It had been weeks since a bona fide hairfall. Had he not witnessed a miracle? How was he to complete the long-delayed bezoar?
With one hand, he clutched the hairs, and with the other, he tugged his beard. He had worked so long to repay his boon from Miss Cindy. The great lady had always supplied the material for his work. He'd thought it certain that this Bezoar would in the end be the finest shrine ever built by gnomish hands.
Now here it lay, unfinished.
Now the golden fleece rained no more.
Now Stig sagged, rubbing his brow.
Might this have been something other than a miracle? The troubling thought crept across his mind. Could the tremor and glow not be taken instead as...as a warning?
Goosebumps stippled his neck.
"No," he said firmly. "I shall not have dark thoughts."
He looked at the wisps of angel hair, frowned.
Maybe--he reshaped his mind around a more hopeful idea, a shrewd expression crawling across his face--I wonder if maybe these few golden strands won't just suffice.
He cursed his faithlessness.
Yes-yesss, that was it! The Lady had provided him with the workings of a true miracle; one to magnify Her glory.
Stig bunched the wisps of hair in his palm, then scoured every oozing surface of the Reflecting until he was certain he had gathered every last hair, long or short, regardless of frizz or fray.
Holding the golden fleece high, and with great reverence, he made a most sincere effort at weaving the them into the Bezoar.
His fingers were deft, fluttering over the split ends, hoping gently to mend and extend them with his stroke.
Trying at it for a long stretch with bated breath, all he succeeded in weaving was a sickly straggle that marred the delicate curlicued surface of the great unfinished bezoar.
Stig frowned.
"That won't do," he muttered into his beard, "No-no n'no! That simply won't do at all."
He put his hand to his face.
"Dearest Cindy, what ever shall I do?"
Lo these long years had he lovingly woven the bezoar--from its first spindly fibers, braiding in humble thanks to the merciful Miss Cindy, whose sacrifice had saved and elevated even as he was smoked out of his previous home.
He closed his eyes and canted gnomish cants.
"One last rain of your angelic fleece would be quite enough, I think," he said to himself. "Enough to adorn your Bezoar with a proper mantle--though it be pitiful, it is holden, I think, of such promise. Such promise."
He turned his face upward.
"A I so unworthy? My Liegess...give me a sign!"
He folded chants into ancient Gnomish tongues, once, twice, thrice--then oncemore, twicemore, thricemore.
And as he began the third three, a rumble rolled from above. The crenelated ceiling bulged inwards.
The ceiling was ever in flux--he gasped--but the scale...


Scene 2. SAD SNUFFLEPUSS

Cindy yanks socks and pillows off the floor, tossing them on the bunk. 
"You're too old for that nasty stuffed animal," says mom.
"I'm not looking for Snuffles, I'm looking for my crocs," Cindy frowns. It's true, she isn't looking for him. She already knows her so-called brothers had thrown him in the laundry again. Stupid jerkwads.
She mopes to the font door where Clay and Leigh and mom eye her expectantly.
"What?" says mom, whose overstuffed raffia bag holds a pair of tan suede crocs. 
"Can I borrow yours?"
"No, you may not," says mom. "Just put on your flip flops and come on."

On the car ride, she is Mme. Laser Fingers, slicing the buildings as they pass, their smooth-cut surfaces sliding languidly apart.
"What are you pointing at?"
"Nothing."
"Then why are you pointing?"
Her laser fingers turn off, the city rests safely again--for now. 

* * * 

She scratches her head, tugging at the short curls.
She could resist the urge to pick and pull if she could just rub her head against her Sad Snufflepuss's sad snuffle.
She winces, remembering every time Larry said that name. He hadn't made the distinction between Cindy and her stuffed snufflepuss, using the name for both of them. And though he was jovial about it, the subtle taunt brittled her.
The name had stuck. Even after she'd rubbed the one-time Pound Puppie into an unrecognizable ball of fluff.
Cindy stretches out on the back seat, kicking Clayton, who pushes her feet away and says "You get back seat next time, Leigh."

* * * 

The orderly pushes her bed past mother and Larry and Clayton and Leigh. The hospital room buzzes morning fluorescent. Cindy absently runs her fingers over her eyebrow hairs, feeling one in particular poking out in the wrong direction.
Clayton and Leigh's customary fight over the front seat is spilling over into the hospital, and mother's glare cuts through the sickly light.
Briefly, Cindy pretends to be scratching her forehead before tucking her hands under the baby blue bedsheets.
Mother is holding Leigh's hand, while her other hand rests gently on Clay's shoulder.
Cindy is ready to get it over with. The angle they have her propped up in the bed makes the uncomfortable feeling under her ribcage all the more pronounced. She presses her hand against her short ribs and rolls the muscles of her abdomen.
Hard to believe the persistent inner nudge will really be gone in a few hours.
"Are they really going to open up my belly?" says Cindy.
Mother rolls her eyes and shoots the orderly a glance. She puts her hand on the bed rail, and says, "What did you expect, Cindy?"
Mom, she almost says.
But then she sees Leigh shooting her a glance. She tries to read her brother's face, but it's stony. He mouths: Shut up, Chewie.
"Mom," she sputters, "Leigh..."
"Oh no you don't," shoots mother. "You leave your brother out of this. You have to take responsibility for your own actions."
Then, with almost a hint of tenderness she adds, "It's time to grow up now. Cind--"
Larry taps mom's shoulder, and waves her away, no doubt to the cafeteria. 
She shakes her head at Cindy then turns to go, leaving Clayton and Leigh to watch over.
Leigh leans in and whispers, "I get pull her stitches out."
Clayton shrugs.

* * * 

Cindy sits alone in the beige and the gray. 
Clickclickclick. She tries to think of a clever comeback to the x-ray machine, but it just clickclickclicks at her again.
"Okay," shouts the nurse from the other room, "one more to go."
Clickclickclick.
Cindy steps out of the x-ray room, taking off the lead-and-plastic apron. She bumps into the Nurse Noris, who's on her way in. 
"Oh!" yelps the nurse, yanking a long, manicured fingernail out of her nostril.
The nurse's smile is so wide her teeth seem perpetually on the verge of coming out of her face, it curls her lip high enough for Cindy to see the bump in the middle of her gums. Cindy stairs at her rainbow hair-scrunchies and savors the cloud of coconut smell wafting around her. A couple of stray orange-crush sparkles sparkle high on her cheeks, and Cindy can imagine her dancing downtown all night with some soft-handed boy.
"It's okay," says Cindy, "I used to pick my nose too--when I was little." 
Cindy smiles, but the nurse's smile fades. 
"Mmmm hmm. Well. Let's get you to your room," says the nurse. 
They walk, and for a second, Cindy is confused because she hears her crocs squeaking even though she's not wearing them. Then she realizes it's not her that's squeaking, it's Nurse Noris. 


Scene 3. TORTURE CHAMBER

The dome undulated above, glistening. Stig patted the medallion, feverishly whispering words whose meanings had long been forgotten. 
Of an instant, a gargantuan silven blade sliced a gash through the dome, narrowly missing Stig's nose--but lopping off a lock of his head hair.
Stig screamed and reflexively snatched up the lock of silver hair, then scuttled into the little alcove behind the Bezoar while the blade sliced forth.
Bracing air flooded in from the gape above. Stig held his palms against the precious Bezoar, shadowed from the harsh outside light. The great blade finished its cut and withdrew. 
Stig hunched over the medallion, rubbing it worrystone-style, the hairs in his hands bristling against its silkenhard surface. He turned his back on the bezoar. Whatever was happening, he didn't want to see.
But even with ducked head, the image of the bezoar in terrifyingly bright light played, awfully, across his inner eye.
He'd been keenly aware that the Bezoar was unfinished. And this queer milky light showed it for true. A big fat felted hairball. He pressed his head on his hands in despair, sobbing lips sparking against the medallion. 
"Oh, the folly," he muttered, "why did I build this bezoar? To so call down such frights upon myself!"
The floor shook, throttling open his eyes.
Through the new hole in the great dome reached a giant set of fingers, their heinous knuckle hairs visible through parchmentlike gloves.
Stig shuddered.
The fingers plunged--obscene--into the grotto, penetrating his holy heart of worship. They clamped down--tightly--terribly--onto the Bezoar.
And they tugged.
Stig's jaw hung slack.
The Bezoar began to rise, its golden lumpiness raining aloft.
No, he thought. "No!" he shouted, fumbling the medallion back into his pocket.
He stood. Astonished, indignant. 
Forgetting his fear, Stig thrust himself forward, digging weaver-thick fingers into the wet fuzz of the Bezoar. He pulled, twisting his hands in the fibers until they seemed permanently bent fistwise. 
But the giant was too strong.
Torn from Stig's grip, it left fistsfuls of clotted angel hair.
When the giant had fully dislodged Stig's Bezoar from its esteemed placement across the Pyloric threshold and the Pool of Light rippled emptily, Stig grasped his hat in disbelief, not bothering to wipe away the droplets splashed upon his face by the bile sluicing from the Bezoar.
He shook both fists.
"It's....not.....FINIIIIIIISHED!" he screamed, righteous anger boiling from his spleen. 
He stomped and cursed, bit his lip...and then...
...he leapt.
Cold air stung his wet face. 
All of his senses: fish-eyed, but crystal clear. 
And he got it! 
The giant wrenched the Bezoar--and Stig along with it--from the sustaining bile he'd called home for years.
Its shiny hand slung them both carelessly into a chill chromen basin. Stig's head thwacked against metal, and he passed briefly into night.
Some moments later, teeth aclatter and echoing against thin metal walls, Stig awoke. 
He stood and spun, seeing nothing but his own distorted reflection. The mirror walls were half again his own height, but he found he could jump and just barely see out of the basin, landing each time with a tinny boot-tink. 
The first jump saw the blade-wielding giant, dressed in periwinkle robe, a mask over its muzzle. On the second, he saw at least two others abreast a long table. And on the third, a hint of curly blonde hair.
Golden Fleece on the head of an angel.
He gasped and ducked behind the still-steaming Bezoar.
The sight of the golden locks--in situ--that is what gave him the strength to do what he did next.
Wincing at the sacrilege, Stig climbed atop the Bezoar and gazed down upon the breathtaking face of his sleeping Miss Cindy, his liegess, lying helpless under the knife of this horrid giant and its gaggle of hench-colossi. An enormous tray of torture implements left no doubt as to their intentions.
