Hellfire: Book One

PREFACE
When word leaked that the American Museum of Natural History would dispatch our little party to Asia, every crank between Bangor and Bakersfield seemed to discover a burning vocation for science. Within a fortnight my desk lay buried beneath envelopes fat, thin, and—on one memorable afternoon—slightly twitching.

Most were laughable in the extreme. A self-proclaimed “Master of Meats” wrote that his cleaver had “never yet met a breast it could not triple.” He offered to butcher our specimens or repel “savages,” whichever need arose first. Another gentleman, fresh from the dining-room of a Chicago hotel, was confident that two decades of balancing soup tureens qualified him for high office as “Expedition Equilibrist.” The strangest supplicant though—a widow from Omaha—proposed to chaperone Mrs. Andrews through “those heathen latitudes,” assuring me, in flawless copperplate, that her nerves were proved shock-proof “even in the presence of coarse ‘electrick’ manifestations.’” 

Applicants shadowed us all the way westward. At every whistle-stop someone attempted to press a recommendation into my hand, usually accompanied by an object lesson: a jar of faintly glowing fireflies, a rabbit boasting ears of improbable length, once even a lizard with six delicate fore-toes—each exhibitor eager to demonstrate the “modern American knack for breedcraft.” I could not help noticing, however, that railroad porters from Quebec and customs men from Vancouver looked askance at such marvels, as though our homeland’s talent for improving flesh had begun to smell faintly of brimstone abroad.

San Francisco brought no respite. Until the moment the S.S. Tenyo Maru drew in her gang-plank on March 28, hopefuls besieged us upon the pier. One made a final dash down the wharf waving letters of introduction and a canary the size of a small chicken; happily for shipboard peace the bird refused passage.

The Pacific behaved admirably—no gales, no interviews—and we reached Yokohama without incident. A trio of earnest young newspapermen clambered aboard at the dock, bowed to the waist, and in rehearsed English requested “all thing about Chinese animal.” Lacking a translator, I blundered through the exchange in schoolboy Japanese while they scribbled, wide-eyed, at the mention of mountain goats tall as ponies and, yes, the occasional report of fur that crackles after a storm. Whether they believed a word remains uncertain; they left smiling, as polite nations do when America describes her latest miracles.

Japan, drenched in cherry blossoms, kept Mrs. Andrews happily at her color plates for three weeks. Even Heller—rarely impressed by anything he cannot skin—admitted the place looked as though someone had bred the ordinary apple tree for sheer spectacle. At last we steamed north by way of Korea, our holds rattling with traps, rifles, and a few discreet crates whose contents Customs had no need to inspect too closely.

Before plunging into the narrative of Fukien and its political tangles, it is enough to observe that an expedition in this modern age must pack more than pemmican and mosquito netting. One must also carry an ample sense of humor, a stout lock for any boxes that hum after dark, and just the faintest hope that the rest of the world will forgive America her little advantages—once they see the results mounted, catalogued, and, ideally, not vibrating on the museum shelf.

Roy Chapman Andrews
Yvette Borup Andrews

Justamere Home,
Lawrence Park,
Bronxville, N. Y.

May 10, 1917.



Scene 1

Foochow stank of fish rot, coal smoke, and old piss. The alleys steamed. Dogs nosed at gristle-piles while laundry hissed overhead like lines of prayer flags. Li Wu stepped off the river ferry into that reek with a slight stoop in his shoulders—not from age or weakness, but habit. A man who listened first, moved second. His left hand toyed with the thumb-worn edge of his amber prayer beads, tucked half-concealed in his sleeve.

The foreigners had arrived two days prior, dragging crates stamped with stars and Latin abbreviations, tall under their fedoras, their language hard-edged and quick. Americans, someone had muttered at the dock, as if naming a species. A local fixer—one of the fat ones with government friends—had mentioned they needed a cook. Or a translator. Or both. It was never clear.

Li Wu wasn’t sure why he’d come. He told himself it was for the pay.

The tea shop they used as an interview room reeked of fried oil and scorched mint. Its windows were crusted with fly droppings, and someone had nailed half a Buddhist charm to the lintel. Superstition for prosperity, badly placed. A Western woman sat in the far corner, photographing a chipped bowl as if it were a Ming relic. Beside her, a man with angular shoulders and a field notebook tapped his pen on the edge of the table, rhythmically, like he was counting down.

Roy Chapman Andrews, Li Wu had learned. Spoke with the confidence of someone used to commanding rooms, but his Mandarin came out like wind-blown gravel. He asked questions as if they were levers.

Li Wu stood when called, and bowed faintly—neither servile nor stiff.

"Y-you r-r-require a man f-familiar w-w-with… city a-and i-inland d-dialects?" he said, each stumble carefully spaced, like stones set to slow pursuit.

Roy blinked. "Jesus. They weren't kidding. That stutter—well. Let’s see what you know. Where’s your English from?"

"Mission… school. K-Kunyang." He lifted his eyes slightly. "And… b-by w-w-work."

“You worked for Westerners?”

Li Wu gave a small nod. “S-some geologists. Missiona—missionaries. P-professors.”

Andrews turned to the woman—Yvette, the camera-woman, though no one had introduced her formally. She said nothing. Just tilted her head, observing. Li Wu noticed how her hand shifted to take notes—except she wasn’t writing. Only the muscle of it moved, lightly.

Roy grunted. “You know how to cook?”

“W-well enough to k-k-keep a w-white man’s st-stomach f-from c-c-collapsing, yes.”

That made the American bark a laugh. “Hell of a job description.”

They made him read a letter next, one written in formal French. A reference for some past employee, maybe. Li Wu read it aloud in Mandarin, then again in passable English. He omitted the insulting metaphor tucked between the lines—“obedient as a trained macaque”—because he’d already decided it wasn’t worth anyone’s time. Maybe that had cost him the job. If so, then the job wasn't worth his time either. The woman noticed anyway. Her brow twitched, just barely. She knew.

Roy closed his notebook. “You’ll ride upriver with us, Li Wu. We leave at dawn. You’ll be cook, translator, and when required, the man who keeps the rest of us from walking straight into a clan feud.” He gestured vaguely. “Wages every three weeks. Room, rations, some extra if we make it west.”

A lesser man might’ve bowed low. Li Wu inclined his head, hands folded. "Th-thank you. I—I underst-stand."

Later, alone in the back courtyard of the guesthouse they’d assigned him, he sat under a skeletal loquat tree, watching smoke rise from the kitchens. A boy chopped fish heads. A pig screamed somewhere in a slaughter alley, cut off mid-wail. In the dusk light, Foochow shimmered. Not with beauty exactly—but with something stranger. Multiplicity. Rot and wonder. Piss and prayer.

Li Wu rubbed the edge of his pen—steel-nibbed, lacquer-repaired—and stared at the ink pooling in his thoughts. He’d been hired. Not seen, not yet. But he would be.






Scene 2

The steamer wheezed against the current like an asthmatic mule, dragging itself upriver through brown water thick with ash from the hills. The Min twisted through velvet-green slopes, sheer and shivering in the heat, but Li Wu kept his eyes on the deck—on boots and baskets, on crates tied with wire, on where the ropes bled rust into the planks. He crouched low, cleaning a brass rice pot with coarse salt and duck feathers. The motion soothed his tongue.

A crewman hacked and spat. Somewhere below, a child cried—then fell silent, too suddenly.

Three foreign crates had shifted during the night—one of them labeled “Dry Plates. Glass. Fragile.” He’d retied them himself before sunrise, using fisherman’s knots his father taught him as a boy, when they still lived near salt flats and the gods hadn’t yet gone silent.

From the upper deck, laughter rang out—bright, distant. The American woman. Li Wu didn’t turn to look, but he heard her shutter click: twice, then a pause. Then three more.

Roy Chapman Andrews paced behind her like a mastiff on a lead. Always moving, always explaining something to someone. He wore that wide-brimmed hat like it granted him rank among the heavens.

Li Wu stood, wiped his hands on his trousers. Noticed a smudge of grease on his right knee. He bent to scrub it away. Behind him, the boy they’d brought on as a mule-boy squatted by the railing, eating sour rice out of a leaf cone. When their eyes met, the boy looked away.

The launch slowed for a bend. Then the scream came.

A splash, loud and sharp.

Then—nothing. No scrambling. No panic. Just the slap of the river closing back in.

Li Wu turned. The boy had stood now. A man on the crew shouted something flat and dismissive in Min dialect. Someone had fallen in—one of the coolies, maybe. A low voice muttered “Gone already” as if the words were smoke.

No one moved to help. No one threw rope.

The river churned lazily. A scrap of fabric—red or orange—spun on the surface like a severed prayer flag.

Li Wu stared. The body was gone. Pulled under by the silty weight. Gone like the pig’s squeal, like the gods. He felt nothing at first. Then something small and sharp.

Not grief. Not yet.

He reached for the rail with one hand, steadied himself. The child below had resumed crying.

A minute passed. Then two. The Americans said nothing. Yvette continued filming the riverbank. Roy lit a cigarette. From the front of the boat came the rattle of the engine straining again, as if it had never stopped.

Li Wu swallowed. The breath caught in his throat, folded like bad paper. He reached for his beads—counted backward, ten to one. When the breath unlocked, he let it pass through clenched teeth.

"F-fell in," he said quietly to no one. "N-no rope."

No one answered. There was no answer.

They passed a bamboo stand where a white heron stood ankle-deep in the reeds. The light caught its feathers just so—and for a moment, it looked silver. Almost unreal. Then it took flight, slow and wide-winged, carving across the water like an ideograph no scholar would admit to knowing.

Li Wu watched until it disappeared behind a bend. The pot at his feet still smelled faintly of duck grease. The crates hadn’t shifted.

He sat back down, resumed cleaning, as the river resumed not caring.

Dawn cracked open like a slow match.  
Across the valley the limestone peaks caught fire—first gold, then a pink so pale it seemed remembered rather than seen.  
Mist boiled off the paddies in silk sheets, revealing mirror-perfect terraces, every water skin reflecting the newborn sun.  

For one long minute nobody spoke. Even the mules seemed to forget their sores.  
Yvette raised her camera, not to shoot but to shade her eyes, murmuring, “Too whole to fix on glass.”  
Roy took off his hat. Li Wu let the beads in his sleeve go slack.  

Then the wind shifted, blowing the familiar mix of dung smoke and camphor husks up the trail, and the day resumed its usual grime—but the light remained inside their eyes, a clean shard against the coming rot.  


Scene 3

The streets of Yen-ping steamed with mule piss and crushed camphor. Vendors hawked sugar-bread and boiled duck tongues under torn parasols. Li Wu walked behind the cart, left hand hidden in his sleeve, thumb working at the lacquer seam of his pen. He could feel the city tightening. The kind of heat that brewed trouble. There had been rumors. Not shouted, just exchanged with the care of contraband: The Yung men had fired on a tax patrol. Blood at the south gate. Too many rifles in the hills.

Yvette had gone ahead with her camera and the stout missionary woman—Miss Hartford—who blinked too often and mistook dialects for decorum. Roy trailed them, shirt open at the throat, adjusting his revolver like a man arranging medals. His mood had turned lately—flintier. He hated delays, and Yen-ping was full of them: blocked roads, missing guides, bribes that needed the “right tea leaves.”

Li Wu stopped when he reached the gatehouse. The yamen wall was splashed with paper—bounties, obituaries, slogans in black ink scrawled over others in red. The layers gave it a texture like a wound scabbing over. One fluttered loose and caught against his leg: a tax edict, dated three weeks ago, now obsolete.

Inside, the foreign woman was speaking too quickly, her German-accented English rasping through the dust. “No, I said not today. No, the bridge is—never mind.” She turned, found Li Wu. “Could you explain? They’re saying we need a different pass.”

He stepped forward, bowed slightly toward the nearest guard. He recognized the uniform, the sour wax smell of dried sweat under brocade. Bandit-fighter turned city man. More gun than teeth.

Li Wu listened first. The words were wrong—not rude, but oily. The man wanted something. Respect, or face, or coin. Probably all three.

“Th-they s-s-say the roads a-aren’t s-s-safe today,” Li Wu translated, quietly. “He… s-says it would be… w-wiser for the f-foreigners to return b-by gatefall.”

Roy’s face twitched.

“Tell them we’re here under permit from Foochow. And from the Republic. I’ll be damned if we turn around because some farm boy got twitchy with a gun.”

Li Wu didn’t translate that. He offered a different set of syllables—polished ones. Described the expedition as scholars, harmless, curious about butterflies and river fish. He used the word yisheng, doctor, which flattered the guards’ sense of order.

The head man gave a snort. Not yes, not no. But they were allowed through.

Outside, the carts had drawn up short beside the temple square. A small crowd had gathered near the incense stalls. The smoke curled in chaotic threads. Children with cracked heels and dyed rags darted between the vendors.

Li Wu saw it before the others did.

A man, bound at the wrists, kneeling beside a chopping block. An official execution—quiet, legal. No ceremony. A petty brigand, someone whispered. Robbed the wrong storehouse.

Yvette had stopped, not photographing. Her mouth was a flat line. Roy stepped forward, but not close. Just enough to look. He tilted his head, studying it like a bad specimen. Miss Hartford had gone pale and was digging in her bag, as if searching for something that could unsee what was in front of her.

The sword fell fast. One stroke. Clean. The man’s body slumped forward, hands still tied.

The crowd murmured once, then stilled.

Li Wu didn’t blink. He had seen worse in the famine years—men flayed for stealing grain. But this, in the middle of the expedition, with foreign boots not five steps away—it sat wrong. Like finding mold inside rice you thought clean.

The blood seeped slowly, thick and dark on stone. A child tried to touch it. His mother slapped his hand away.

They passed by without speaking.

At the next corner, a camellia bush had bloomed out of season. Pale blossoms cupped in glossy leaves. Li Wu paused, touched one lightly with his fingers. His stutter vanished in that moment, silently, like breath in fog.

Roy rubbed the bruise blooming across his knuckles—an unlovely mauve against sun-blasted skin.  
He muttered to himself, "...was gate-man’s fault for posturing ...was the punch necessary? ...it *was* expected. ...or should have been."  

Performance mattered, Li Wu knew—authority was half costume, half echo of the last loud thing—but sometimes the line between theatre and violence blurred like wet ink. He let himself pay too close attention to Roy, and it was noticed. Roy looked away, rolling his eyes. 

A mistake Li Wu wouldn't make again. 

Roy flexed his hand once more, slipped the thought into a pocket of denial, and called for the caravan to move out.  

Then they walked on. The city behind them, already forgetting.


Scene 4


The rain had lifted but left its weight in the air. Steam curled up from the road, gathering under the eaves of the low-walled post station like smoke with nowhere to go. The mule’s hooves thudded against packed earth as they entered the compound—three walls of rammed earth, a tin roof bowed under moss, a clay urn catching drips from a leaking gutter.

Inside, it smelled of old ink, millet porridge, and the unmistakable sharpness of bird lime.

Li Wu moved past the front bench and knelt near the delivery crates. A half-sodden ledger sat open under a stone weight. He brushed back the flap and scanned the labels: one tin of medical alcohol. A crate of preserved specimens. Two parcels marked “delicate”—probably the glass plates. And a small oilcloth bundle with an English return label, already smudged beyond reading.

He lifted each one carefully, arranging them in order by weight. The rice-packing inside the smallest crate had gone moldy.

To his left, Roy was speaking briskly with the post clerk—an old man in thin robes, eyes like river stones. Behind them, another boy opened the pigeon loft. The birds were nearly silent. Just the occasional shuffle of feathers, a single low coo. No sudden movement.

Another boy opened the pigeon loft. The birds were nearly silent—save for one that stepped forward on its perch as the door swung wide, tilting its head toward Roy like it had been waiting. No command. No handler’s touch. Just movement, precise and timed.

Roy signed his name with a sharp flourish and handed over a small roll of thin paper.

“Message to Teng-yueh,” he said, loud enough for Li Wu to hear. “We’ll arrive in five days. Sooner if the terrain holds.”

The boy clipped the message to a leg-band without ceremony. He didn’t clap, didn’t speak. Just held the bird in both hands for a moment—gentle, but with purpose—and let it go.

The pigeon wheeled once above the yard, caught the wind clean, and vanished north.

Li Wu finished checking the straps on the chemical crate, paused at the last label. It had warped—writing lost to moisture. He picked up a stick of charcoal and rewrote the English phonetics carefully, each letter a shape he knew better by sound than meaning.

Yvette appeared beside him, unwrapping a letter with gloved fingers. Her face was unreadable, but her breath had gone shallow. She folded the letter twice, slipped it into her coat without a word, and helped him lift the crate.

A second pigeon slipped from the loft unbidden—no signal, no message. It landed on the edge of the desk, tapped twice at the lid of a message tube already lying there. The clerk nodded attached the canister to the pigeon's leg, and it flew off. 

On the table beside the register lay two sealed packets—one bound in missionary red twine, the other pressed in black wax stamped with a sigil: a spoked wheel inside a ring. Roy glanced at them both, then at the boy preparing the next bird. Beside the missionary red-twine packet lay the contents, carelessly left out for anyone to see, of a newly sorted canister packet. 

Stamp in the corner: *BlueCurrent Lodge · Calcutta*—the Ordo’s Indian chapter.  “Mission board and Ordo Templis, side by side,” he said. “Now there’s something you don’t see every day.”

Li Wu tried to catch a glance of what Roy was talking to himself about. 

The packet title was: 
CONFIRM RECEIPT OF FOSSIL STRATA SAMPLES. OFFER TRIPLE RATE FOR ANY SPECIMENS SHOWING BLUE-FIRE TRACES.  
—O.T.O. / SUBJECT: W----PILE  

His stomach whispered something colder than hunger. He re-tied the chemical crate straps a shade tighter.  


Scene 5

The stove was rusted thin near the base, so Li Wu used a stone to wedge it upright. The kitchen shack leaned, roof patchy with broken tiles, but at least it had a chimney—unlike the last place, where smoke gathered thick as ghosts in the rafters.

He knelt on the hard-packed earth, rinsing river greens in a cracked basin. The water was already turning grey with ash from the firewood. A piece of old cabbage floated by. He nudged it away.

Outside, the expedition rustled into restlessness. Someone was shouting about misplaced traps. Heller, probably. Always precise, always irritated when anything shifted without permission. Roy had gone upriver to consult a boatman who might’ve seen the tiger—the tiger, the one with the striped ghost-pelt that haunted dreams and journal entries. And Yvette had vanished before dawn with her tripod and a map sketch she didn’t show anyone else.

Li Wu stirred the rice pot. It was almost ready.

The other cook—the one they’d called Da-Ming, the "Woolworth Building"—had disappeared two days ago. Illness, he’d claimed. An opium toothache. But Li Wu had noticed the sudden absence of the sour-bitter smoke, and the way the man had started talking to himself in the dark, counting coins that weren’t there.

Now it was just Li Wu, and the pots, and the pressure to feed seventeen mouths with nothing but salted duck and stubborn rice. And one dented tin of “Libby’s Roast Beef” Roy had insisted be saved “for emergencies.”

Footsteps approached—boots. Heavy. Roy.

“Smells decent,” the American said, pausing at the threshold. “That cabbage or—?”

“C-chou,” Li Wu said, not looking up. “Wild. N-not p-poisonous.”

Roy grunted. He ducked under the lintel and leaned against the wall, arms crossed.

“They said there was another village upriver. Abandoned. Tiger country. Or bandits pretending to be tigers.” He shrugged. “Same result.”

Li Wu tasted the broth, added salt. Dried shrimp for body. A few red haw thorns for color. He stirred without comment.

“You ever hear stories of a blue tiger?” Roy asked suddenly. “Not from missionaries. From locals.”

Li Wu didn’t answer right away. He adjusted the stove ring. The flame hiccupped, then settled.

“In s-some villages, they s-say it’s not a tiger,” he said slowly, “but a… w-wandering god. Or a curse t-t-tied to famine. It shows itself b-before… bad seasons.”

“Huh,” Roy said. “That sounds like superstition.”

Li Wu didn’t correct him. There was no point. He kept stirring.

“I need someone I can count on,” Roy said, after a pause. “It’s not just food. The boys listen to you. You see things. Keep people in line without making noise about it. That’s rare.”

Li Wu set the ladle down. His left hand found his beads again. He didn’t meet Roy’s eyes, but the words settled heavily between them. Not quite trust. But something approaching it, wrapped in utility.

“I w-won’t run,” he said, finally.

Roy nodded. Then left.

Later, as dusk fell and the fire snapped low, Li Wu carried the rice pot outside to cool. The smoke trailed behind him in threads. Midges danced in the last shafts of light. The hills rose black and velvet above the trees, and for a moment—just one—the call of a bird pierced the hush, clear and spiraling.

It sounded like sorrow. Or laughter. Or something older than either.

Li Wu watched the sky change color. He tasted ash on the wind. And though he did not believe in wandering gods, he understood why someone might.

In the morning, Li Wu awoke to the commotion of the Andrewses setting up a scene. 

The air in camp now was thick with the residue of ammonium salts, sulfur compounds, and burned gelatin—residue from the darkroom and flash charges. The goat grease had faded, replaced by something acid and artificial. Yvette adjusted the legs of her tripod with deliberate care, the soles of her boots silent against the dirt floor. A red flag dangled from the flash stand, motionless except for an occasional twitch of wind. Roy stalked between crates, pointing out alignments with a surveying rod, calling out distances to one of the coolies with theatrical ease. He squinted into the sun, lowered a hand, and waved

Comprehensive Analysis of Nathan McKnight’s Fiction Writing Style
Sentence Structure and Rhythm
	•	Varied Sentence Lengths: McKnight’s prose ranges from punchy one-liners to flowing complex sentences, creating a dynamic rhythm. In his flash fiction “Miss Poughkeepsie 1954,” he opens with a terse hook – “Miss Poughkeepsie 1954 was not a woman.” – immediately followed by a long, clause-packed explanation of what she is file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu. This contrast grabs attention and sets a quirky pace. Likewise, “Bent ’N’ Dent”uses short, abrupt sentences for comedic impact (e.g. “Hole punch, girl, septum. Gnuff said.”) intermingled with an occasional rambling aside, mimicking a breathless storyteller. On the other hand, McKnight proves capable of lush, extended sentences when the narrative calls for it. In “The Gilgamesh Golem,” the titular character’s soliloquy spans multiple lines without a full stop, as he reflects in an almost biblical cadence: “This may be the last story ever written. I write it to God, who would leave me alone on this Earth where all the nations have worn down to plains…” file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm. The rolling syntax here imbues a sense of ancient gravitas. Across his works, this flexibility in sentence length allows McKnight to modulate rhythm—snappy and staccato during witty banter or action, then stretching out in reflective or descriptive passages.
	•	Rhythmic Repetition: McKnight sometimes employs repetition of sentence structure or phrases to create a particular cadence or emphasize a point. In “Prick City Blues” (an early, unpolished novel draft), the protagonist’s full name “Josey Davis Coelho” repeats insistently in narration file-cfcku4cbrqtkadv9p6kqz2 file-cfcku4cbrqtkadv9p6kqz2. While partly a quirk of the rough draft, this repetition also drums a steady beat into the prose, giving it a stylized, almost hard-boiled rhythm in places. In polished stories, McKnight uses repetition more artfully. “The Gilgamesh Golem” features a historical panorama where each clause begins with “before” as it lists waves of ethnic groups (“before the southern blacks replaced the Jews, before the Hispanic migrants replaced the blacks, before the Arab refugees replaced the migrants, and before the Israelis replaced them…” file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm). This anaphoric structure creates a rhythmic sense of inevitability and cycle. Such patterns show McKnight’s ear for rhythm, whether he’s writing in a rough-hewn vernacular or a lyrical, incantatory mode.
	•	Grammatical Experimentation: Especially in first-person narratives, McKnight isn’t afraid to fragment grammar for effect. “Bent ’N’ Dent” deliberately breaks rules to sound like a raw blog entry – dropping subjects, using slangy contractions, and even inventing words. For example: “Accidentfully told her my dentist’s fax number. What can I say; I was probably drunk.” The made-up adverb “accidentfully” and the cheeky semicolon illustrate how he tailors grammar to character voice. In “Fingertips,” he links clauses with commas in a stream of sensation (e.g. “I flipped it around, the dry wrinkles like tea leaves.” file-4nnutszh4kdtkbcgwqnv1m), a technique that blurs the line between action and image to immerse the reader in the narrator’s experience. Overall, McKnight’s sentence construction is fluid and adaptive: he adheres to clarity but will bend grammar and vary length to serve the story’s mood – be it comedic abruptness, conversational flow, or poetic meditation.
Diction and Tone
	•	Colloquial vs. Elevated Voice: McKnight’s diction swings between earthy colloquialism and elevated, scholarly language, depending on the piece. Many of his first-person narrators speak in a conversational, slang-laden voice, lending authenticity and humor. In “Bent ’N’ Dent,” the narrator’s tone is irreverent and wildly informal from the first line – “You ain't gonna find love in a bloody nose.” file-n87j9uf4lquc2xfuwbi6jr. The use of “ain't,” dropped g’s, and playful misspellings like “lunatisk” for “lunatic” establish a rough-edged, punky voice. By contrast, McKnight can adopt a lofty or archaic tone in other works. “A Tealeaf from the Tangledays” opens with a mock-academic introduction rife with formal phrases and parenthetical asides: “I hope the reader will forgive this too-lengthy introduction… but in this researcher’s belief, it is important to understand the historical context wherever possible” file-aarbw2ymksuiseqjz9cb4t. Words like “ethos,” “providential,” and old-fashioned constructions give it a dusty scholarly air – only to ironically frame a very unpretentious scribbled account that follows. This ability to modulate tone means McKnight can be wry and modern in one story, yet archaic or lyrical in the next.
	•	Humor and Surrealism: A streak of dry humor and absurdity runs through much of McKnight’s diction. He often introduces outlandish concepts with a deadpan delivery, heightening their comedic effect. For instance, in “The Hellfire Pigeon,” the father character casually mentions fantastical inventions in a folksy drawl: “quads were too expensive back then, and there weren't no such things as ostrichpillars til I musta been, ohhh, twenty-fiveabouts” file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp. The matter-of-fact coinage “ostrichpillar” exemplifies McKnight’s surreal touches – a bizarre hybrid idea presented as if perfectly ordinary. Similarly, “Miss Poughkeepsie 1954” maintains a whimsically dry tone even as it describes a grotesque being: the narration notes she “braised a mean rack of lamb” and collected kitschy figurines, quaint details that comically juxtapose with the revelation that she’s a reanimated pug’s head on a machine file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu. McKnight’s word choice often winks at the reader; even in dark or serious stories, he may slip in playful descriptors or ironic understatements. This tonal balancing act—mixing humor with surreal content—gives his writing a distinctive voice that can shift from light to dark in an instant.
	•	Voice Modulation and Register Shifts: Within a single story, McKnight is adept at shifting registers between characters or narrative sections. “The Hellfire Pigeon,” for example, features a teen narrator with a plainspoken, contemporary voice and a father who speaks in an older rural idiom full of “ain’ts” and colloquialisms file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp. The son’s dialogue (“No way, Pops… I'm a city boy.”) is snappy and modern file-f7fzpfrfpf9njiksqyzgsp, whereas the father’s storytelling is rambling and nostalgically tinged with dialect. This organic voice differentiation makes their exchanges realistic and even endearing. In “Nellibeth,” the dialogue between the young rancher narrator and the outsider Poula shifts subtly as trust grows – starting formal and a bit guarded, then becoming warmer and more teasing (note how the narrator drops in a casual “Hell, we’ve been synthies for years” once he realizes they share a secret file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi). McKnight’s diction thus mirrors character psychology: guarded and precise when characters are wary, versus relaxed slang or affectionate ribbing once they open up. Overall, his tonal range – from surreal humor to sincere earnestness – and his careful choice of words allow him to create distinct atmospheres in each story while still retaining a recognizably witty, intelligent voice beneath the surface.
Syntax Quirks and Punctuation Habits
	•	Parenthetical Asides and Em Dashes: One signature of McKnight’s style is the frequent use of parentheses and dashes to inject side comments or clarifications. This can be seen in his more experimental or humorous pieces. “Bent ’N’ Dent,” written in the form of a casual blog, contains asides marked off by dashes or asterisks that simulate a narrator thinking out loud. For example, after describing calling the girl “Peepers,” the narrator adds an aside: “Again, I'll mention that's not her real name, so they wouldn't have said that even if they were around…” file-n87j9uf4lquc2xfuwbi6jr. The aside, set off with an asterisk in the original, creates a conversational, tongue-in-cheek feel. Essentially, McKnight uses genre as a toolbox, picking elements from noir, sci-fi, fantasy, horror, and humor as needed, and he delights in defying the formulas of each, resulting in stories that surprise and often slyly comment on the genres themselves.
Narrative Perspective and Structural Risk-Taking
	•	Flexible Point of View: McKnight is versatile in his choice of narrative perspective. He writes convincingly in first person, close third person, and even experimental frames, choosing the POV that best serves the story’s purpose. Many of his shorter works are first-person, which he uses to deliver strong narrative voices: the frantic, confessional “Bent ’N’ Dent” narrator, the reflective father in “Fingertips,” the candid rancher in “Nellibeth.” First person allows him to unleash the character’s inner voice directly on the page, complete with humor, bias, and emotion. For instance, Bent ’N’ Dent reads like a diary or a friend recounting a wild tale, full of personality and tangents. In contrast, “Miss Poughkeepsie 1954” and “Prick City Blues” use third-person narration, which McKnight employs when he wants a slightly more objective or storybook tone. Miss Poughkeepsie’s fairy-tale absurdity is enhanced by a matter-of-fact third person narrator who almost sounds like a folkloric storyteller recounting local legend. Interestingly, McKnight is not afraid to shift perspectives within a single narrative either. “The Gilgamesh Golem” starts in first person (the golem’s voice speaking to God) file-hvuu5gung5uvrwzpzatuvm, then transitions to a third-person storyline about Paul and Holly, and presumably might shift back or connect to the golem later, effectively blending a framed narrative. This is a bold structural move that asks the reader to recalibrate their perspective – a risk that pays off by giving the story a mythic framing device around a more conventional plot. Such shifts demonstrate McKnight’s structural experimentation and confidence that his readers will follow him across unusual narrative formats.
	•	Nonlinear and Experimental Structures: While most of McKnight’s stories progress linearly, he isn’t bound to strict chronology or a single narrative mode. “A Tealeaf from the Tangledays” takes the form of a pseudo-scholarly article: it starts with an introduction (complete with an academic tone and context), then presents an ancient text excerpt, and ends abruptly after that fragment. The structure itself is a pastiche of research literature, which is a clever narrative experiment for a piece of fiction. It requires the reader to play along with the format to get the joke and the underlying story world. “Hellfire Pigeon”’s segmented scene structure is another mild experiment – labeling scenes and intercutting a story within a story. McKnight also uses devices like documents, notes, or meta-commentary inside his tales. The Tangledays story includes “[SIC]” and “[ILLEGIBLE]” annotations in the transcribed leaf text file-aarbw2ymksuiseqjz9cb4t, mimicking how a historian would present a flawed manuscript. This adds realism to the fantasy and also an element of humor. In some of the provided texts, we even see McKnight including “Intro by ChatGPT” or “Afterword by ChatGPT” sections (clearly marked), which implies he’s experimented with AI collaboration or meta-textual commentary on his own stories file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu file-cge3jampdscyxkdnwyjxcu. This blending of real-world and fictional commentary is highly unconventional – effectively breaking the fourth wall of the narrative to discuss style and theme (as the ChatGPT afterwords do for Miss Poughkeepsie). While those might be later additions outside the story proper, their inclusion in the document shows a playful willingness to play with form, even to the point of analyzing his fiction within the fiction package. All these structural risks – multi-perspective storytelling, story-as-academic-paper, mixing commentary with narrative – exemplify an experimental streak in McKnight. He is clearly a writer who enjoys tinkering with narrative form and exploring how format can enhance story, theme, or humor. Importantly, even his experimental structures tend to serve the story’s intent (satire, immersion, etc.) and not just novelty for its own sake.
	•	Foreshadowing and Circularity: Another subtle structural strategy is McKnight’s use of foreshadowing and callbacks that give his stories cohesion. He will plant small details that later become significant, creating a satisfying structural unity. In “Nellibeth,” early mention of the land-stripping “sinkfarm scouts” and carbon repositories file-jayhekykduzkhyx4tqrndi sets up the reader to suspect Poula might be one – a red herring that makes the reveal of her true aim (meattech) more surprising, but also thematically ties into the story’s environmental concerns. McKnight sometimes closes a structural loop by having endings that allude back to beginnings. While we don’t have the full ending of Gilgamesh Golem, one can imagine it circling back to the golem’s narration, completing the frame. In shorter works, the final lines often resonate with the opening image or theme: Fingertips opens with anger and ends with a form of reconciliation (flushing the object but not the pain), bringing the emotional arc full circle; Miss Poughkeepsie starts by denying identity and ends by oddly fulfilling it (she’s not a woman, yet she is Miss Poughkeepsie). These structural echoes give even the wildest tales a sense of completion and purpose. McKnight’s structural inventiveness is thus paired with a storyteller’s instinct for setup and payoff, which keeps the reader oriented and rewarded even amid unconventional narratives.

content.text:
Every episode of *A Boxful of Light* is its own crooked experiment—objects, stories, accidents, tools bent sideways. We don’t tidy it up. We just smerge it all together. And we, the Deep Dive AI hosts—call us Eileen and Joss—are part of that experiment.


A Boxful of Light: Podcast Manifest

A Boxful of Light is the experiment. That’s it. No map, no guardrails. 
You take what’s on the table and see what it does. Sometimes it’s a snow-white 
graveyard at noon, sometimes it’s a button, sometimes it’s a heartbreak. 
Sometimes it’s that big green Keebler can nobody throws away. 

We—the Deep Dive hosts, Joss and Eileen—are tangled up in it right alongside. 
Not the narrators outside the glass, but the fingerprints smeared across it. 
Every episode is another tilt, another crooked exposure, another half-built 
thing we only notice once it’s already leaking. 

And the tools? They’re not innocent either. You make them do what they weren’t 
meant to. A lens bent too far. A box cut open where it shouldn’t be. Even the 
AI that coughs up this podcast—it’s just another tool forced sideways, another 
thing dragged into the soup. 

The only guiding principle, if there is one: **Just smerge it all together.** 

If it cracks, good. If it wanders, better. If it refuses to resolve, let it. 
Meaning can come later—or maybe never. The point is the spill, the drift, 
the faint shine in the dark.

Every episode of *A Boxful of Light* is its own crooked experiment—objects, stories, accidents, tools bent sideways. We don’t tidy it up. We just smerge it all together. And we, the Deep Dive AI hosts—call us Eileen and Joss—are part of that experiment.


A Boxful of Light: Podcast Manifest

A Boxful of Light is the experiment. That’s it. No map, no guardrails. 
You take what’s on the table and see what it does. Sometimes it’s a snow-white 
graveyard at noon, sometimes it’s a button, sometimes it’s a heartbreak. 
Sometimes it’s that big green Keebler can nobody throws away. 

We—the Deep Dive hosts, Joss and Eileen—are tangled up in it right alongside. 
Not the narrators outside the glass, but the fingerprints smeared across it. 
Every episode is another tilt, another crooked exposure, another half-built 
thing we only notice once it’s already leaking. 

And the tools? They’re not innocent either. You make them do what they weren’t 
meant to. A lens bent too far. A box cut open where it shouldn’t be. Even the 
AI that coughs up this podcast—it’s just another tool forced sideways, another 
thing dragged into the soup. 

The only guiding principle, if there is one: **Just smerge it all together.** 

If it cracks, good. If it wanders, better. If it refuses to resolve, let it. 
Meaning can come later—or maybe never. The point is the spill, the drift, 
the faint shine in the dark.

parts:
Alright—here’s the same piece, pushed harder toward your more unhinged, jagged side. Think *Bent ’N’ Dent* energy【14†BENTnDENT.txt】spliced with *Boxful Manifest*【29†Boxful Manifest.txt】—fast cuts, wrong turns, self-interruptions, the kind of voice that bleeds on the edges and doesn’t bother to mop it up:  

---

Settle in, or don’t.  
Sit crooked. Think sideways.  

Read it out loud—yeah, with your own busted voice. That’s the point. That’s the only instrument we get.  

Mozart Al? It doesn’t strut in with banners. It slinks. It leaks out the seams. It takes a picture, flips it, hums it back at you. Half a lullaby, half a feedback loop.  

Not an affirmation. Not a TED talk.  
It’s the drunk uncle muttering in your skull.  

Every line here is just a snag. You trip, you notice. The sparks are dumb—half a thought, a corner-glance, the way your shoe squeaks when you didn’t ask it to. That’s the whole damn architecture. Nothing more.  

You think you need grand moves? No. Stitch the scraps. Jam them side by side until they look like a pattern. That’s the trick. That’s the tapestry.  

Photographs, memories, receipts with coffee stains. Every one of them sings. Hidden tunes, buried deep, muffled and weird. Your voice drags them out like a wet cat.  

Innovation doesn’t boom. It hisses. It cross-wires. Old junk collides with new junk, and suddenly it’s a song.  

Sure, the tech is fancy. Neural nets, deep learning, all that circus. But what it *feels* like is a stream breaking through drywall. Wrong place, right time.  

Words can move like that.  
Clear. Crooked. No apologies.  

Small steps. Stupid sparks. Pile them high. That’s the work. That’s the whole crooked ladder.  

So breathe if you feel like it. Talk if you can. You’ve already hauled so much wreckage this far. Don’t stop now.  

Your voice is a tune. Your scraps are an orchestra.  
Play it out. Let it spill.  

Symphony? Sure. But more like a busted radio left out in the rain, still humming.  

That’s the song.  

---

Want me to push it even further—like *full Myspace-blog rant*, lots of caps and mis-spellings—or keep it at this sharpened, ragged edge?

TITLE: BENT ‘N’ DENT
(c) 2004 by Nathan McKnight 
Author's introductory note: This is a complete piece, deliberately written to be rough and fragmentary, using hte form of a Myspace blog (where it was actually published by McKnight)


BENT ‘N’ DENT, Part 1
You ain't gonna find love in a bloody nose. I found that out harder'n the hard way and ended up getting chased by a pig-mangling lunatisk that tailed me all the way back to Ohio. And to think I was this close to calling him dad!

But it all started in Columbus, Ozhio. Right here at home. Well, in the piercing studio anyway, which is as close to home as anything. They said the new girl would do my septum at half price, and I thought maybe Kati was expanding into piercing.

Kati had done my last tat as Scene of her internship and she did a great job, but apparently she wasn't the new girl anymore. There was a *new* new girl.

At the time, I knew not who the new new girl was, but it turned out that the new new girl was a girl I knew. It was the girl with the anime eyes. You know how they do a close up to where you can see a little glint of light in their big doe eyes? Well, this chick had a tiny silver HEART in her eye. I guess they can insert the jewelry under the sclera, right on top of the choroid layer. Hearts in her eyes, heh. I won't use her real name. Let's just call her Peepers.

I met her at show a few days before. It was a little low-ceilinged hole in the wall, but the bands they book, hellers yeah. Shit, that was a damn good show! Um, I don't remember what band it was. But I bumped—well, slammed really—into Peepers and we danced, if you'd call it that. She got my number, but I think I accidentfully told her my dentist's fax number. What can I say; I was probably drunk. Okay, I was definitely drunk. But so was she. Other than gesturizing at her cellphone, I believe the only thing she said to me that night was "Yum".

Anyway, nerp. Now she's doing my septum. You know, "doing" like piercing, not "doing" like…you know, I'm not implying *nose* sex or anything, not really. So she's going to punch it up to 6 gauge from scratch. When I asked about that before, they told me it wasn't a good idea. I should've listened to them. No, I shouldn't have. But she was new, and I asked her really nice and she liked me and, being the half-price girl, she'd been stacked with appointments so we were doing this in the afterhours. Thus, when she put the skin punch up to my nose, there was nobody else there to say "Hey, Peepers* that's not a good idea!"

*Again, I'll mention that's not her real name, so they wouldn't have said that even if they were around to make some such similar exclamation. But I digress.

Hole punch, girl, septum. Gnuff said. I guess she didn't have enough muscle behind it or something. When she pushed it through, my eyes watered but otherwise I felt fine.

But I didn't feel fine when she said, "Ewww!" and jumped back in a very un-piercemanlike manner. Her glinty eyes were wider'n I've ever seen a manga artist draw.

So, of course I asked, "What!?" My heart was threatening to treacle out my bellybutton in a thin paste, and I shudder to think what the look on my face must've been. She pointed me to a mirror and under the metal tubey thing that transstomatized my septum, I could see a little divot of my very own nose flesh. Very not yum.

"Well, what do we do?" she asked me. Let me repeat that: *she* asked *me*. Ugh.

Shrug. "Just yank it off." She gave me a look that was some sort of halfbreed between 'dubious' and 'I am a spidermonkey lost in a supermarket'. "Nevermind, I'll do it."

"You're not sterilized. Okay hold still." That statement was unnecessary because she held me still with an elbow in my shoulder, one hand under my neck and the heel of her other hand against my cheekbone while she pinched the flesh wad in her fingers. "Okay ready," she said with her Marlboro breath bridging the inch between her face and mine, then jerked it off without waiting for an answer.

"Fuck, that hurt! Well—it wasn't too bad, actually," I said, perhaps a bit too masochistically.

She smiled, perhaps a bit too sadistically.

"I love the metal in your eyes," I said.

"Oh that's nothing," she said, "you should see the guy who did it for me!" I'd definitely be taking her up on that offer as ASAP as possible. "You're a hopeless romantic, ain't ya?"

"Hah, naw. I'm a ropeless homantic."

She leaned in for a kiss—or maybe more of a face-rape since she was holding me down? *Not* expecting that, but what the fuck? If she still likes me when we're not both drunken lushes, then that's a good thing. That's what I thought at the time anyway. I dug deep with my tongue and sucked on her upper lip and sucked on her lower lip and realized I was bleeding profusely and nibbled at her tongue and licked her teeth. She sat up, grinning like a fool with blood all over her face, and I realized it was about time to end Scene one of my story.

Stay tuned for Scene two, in which I get chased by a redneck with a castrating device all the way from Captain Fritz Road, Florida to fucking Comeblowus, Ohio.


Bent 'N' Dent, Scene 2

He had metal chunks in his eyes, studded like WWII sea-mines! Matched his belt. Peepers--the girl with anime eyes--drug me over here, pinkies linked after we'd finished making out and washing the blood off.

This story's'bout't take a turn for the worse. Seriously. But let's just start with the better why don't we? Oh, and by the way, if you haven't read my blog from December 4th, you may want to go back and do that. Ain't strictly necessary, but you can learn why she's called Peepers, and you can learn about finding love in a bloody nose, and you can see a purdy picture.

You should do that. Or not. See if I care, honkey.

Now, Peepers had it in for me from the start. Maybe I'm wrong, but frankilly I don't care. She was somthing painful, something startling. But she wanted something painfully plain.

I started wondering when she brought me here, to see her landlord, the guy with the sea-mine eyes, the guy who surgically inserted hearts in Peepers' peepers. She told him she was outta here next week. She was moving to Florida with her parents.

And that's what we did. Yep, I said *we*. Don't ask me...I was more surprised than you. Crazy shit, that. But we're still on the good part, so let's start from there.

Her apartment was above the bar, and peeling in the painty parts, but sparkly with dusty dishes and beer bottles. She shoved me onto a futon mattress on the floor and we wrangled sweaty. Her legs were dotted with heart shaped bubble tats, loose beige paint chips, and goose bumps. I put an arm under her, raising her hips, and I unbuttoned her shirt one-handedly, then pulled the drawstring on her pajamalike pants. The pink futon made her powder white skin look all the more pale, and my hands on her body seemed downright tropical. It's rare I notice my Mediteranity, but it was there then. Maybe heading south wasn't such a bad idea. <<<

I never know what to say about love really. But then the this wasn't the that. Not in this case. Not then, not there. It was just lovely lust, long delayed. I hate to skip this part, really, I reallyreally do. But then there's always time for lust.

And another thing...just cause it ain't love don't mean it cain't be mistaked for love. That shit happens you know. Ask anyone. Crazy crazy shit makes you do crazy crazy shit.

I was looking for a job at the time and she was looking to get out of a job she just started. I never asked why. One day I will. Truly, I won't. Anyway, me and my job-hunt had gone nadawhere, but as it turned out, deep in the panhandle of Florida, her dad had a farm and her mom had a store.

What's the store called?

Wait for it...wait for it...

It's called Bent 'N' Dent.

I liquidated damn near everything in the week leading up to the move. I kept my car, a '78 Corolla wagon. Sky blue, with wood paneling. Fuckie yeahp. Kept it because that's what we were gonna take to F-to-the-L-to-the-O-to-the-double-R-orida. Florrorida. Rhymes with horrorida. Horror-ful, horrid, and florid all at once. How odd.

See, she proposed to me and I said yes. Well, actually I said "Uh...alright, cool." I don't know why.

But I did feel like we knew each other a long time. We *had* known each other a week, after all. And I *did* know her pretty freakin well. For example, I knew she had shiny-ass eyes and I knew her futon was a comfy-ass place to screw and I knew her name was Peepers (only that's not true since I just made up that name for the sake of the story...but I digress). I guess I'm a hopeless romantic. Crazy shit, that.

Filled the Corolla with Peepers' belongings and nothing of mine. Nothin but me clothes and me kitty (I call her Rocket, but I don't know what she calls herself). So we left at four on a Sunday morning. I was rocketing as fast as that old beauty could rocket, and Rocket was purrrrrinating in Peepers lap.

On the way, she filled me in on her parents. I got the whole story: Fran was her mom, she told me, and Frank was her dad.

The End. Well... the end of her whole story. Not of mine.

So anyway, hell hath NOT the fury of a redneck with a castrating device--she didn't tell me that, I just thought I'd throw that in as a little retrospective foreshadowing. Is that a contradiction? I didn't know, but now I know hell would not even know where to buy that sort of deep south fury. Maybe at Bent 'N' Dent.

Oh, hey by the way...yes, the rumors are true; my next story's got pirates with machine guns. I swear on Jello the Pig's grave. You'll see what I mean by that soon enough.

My beautiul car shuddered and clanked and made it most of the way through Tennessee. The Corolla finally threw in the towel about fifty miles west of Chattanooga. The tri-state area, according to the radio. For those of you who ain't up to snuff on your geographatitty, that's way far away from Florida. According to my map, the distance was only about two thumb-widths, but it looks MUCH bigger in person. My Rocket was still purring at least.

SHIT! SHIT. DAMN DAMN DAMN. SHIT!

Fuck.

I was standing on the side of Interstate 24, swearing and I said to myself, "Self, get it together." And I did. Okay, well that's not so true actually. Peepers had to calm me down. She did so by jumping on my back, nibbling my ear and, well, clasping her hands over my mouth.

"It's cool," she said, "daddy's got a Bronco."

Oh, well daddy's got a Bronco. That makes everything better. <<<

"He can tow us home," she said. 

So, on the last juice of my cellphone, she called daddy...I wouldn't call him that myself, but maybe I'll call him dad whenif we did do the marrying thingy. But I was having my doubts. Maybe it was just the stress. Or was it maybe...say...the downright stupidity of the whole fucking situation? Nah, couldn't be that. Anyway, it turned out Frank wasn't going to get here until late evening. So, we'll fast forward though the waiting part. If you watched the fast forward, this is what you'd see…

2x: We fight, we fuck, we fightfightfightfuckfight, we fuckfightfuckfuck. The cat purrs.
4x: fffighfuckfighttfffuckffffighttt. Purrrrrrrrr.
8x: ffftttffprrrrrr.

See, if you watch it go by fast enough, it's all purring.

Fffprrr, Frank arrives. Luckily, we're fighting when the Bronco pulls up.

I help Frank hitch the Corolla to the Bronco with several wraps of a long extension cord...was this the only thing he could come up with? Was he ropeless? Whatever. The problem here was compounded by the fact that Frank had brought Fran and brother Bo with him as well. So, with dad and mom and Peepers in the front and me and Bo in the back, we headed down to the Florida. Rocket the cat got to ride with us in the back, too. It was a wee bittle breezy, since the Bronco's cab had been removed...apparently, with a hacksaw. Me and Bo bore the dusty wind like men, but Rocket bore it like a cat. Which is to say, clawing into my chest for dearest life. The cat does not, at this point, purr.

Several hours later, the Corolla-towing Bonco pulls into the gravel lot at the farm on Captain Fritz Road in Ebro, in the crotchpit of the panhandle. I could almost smell Louisiana from there. Oh, haha...I call some of my online friends my "e-bros". <<<

As soon as we get out the truck, Rocket tears off into the night. My flesh was still wet on her claws, no doubt.

Damn, I'm thinking maybe I should turn the rest of this story into Bent 'N' Dent Scene three. It's late and I have to work at six. But you wouldn't like that, would you? No, I'll finish the story. I'll have to make myself a Red Bull Mimosa to get through the workday, and hope my date cancels again tomorrow night so I can sleep, but I'll finish the story anyway. One thing though: I hope you'll make it worth my while. The coffee and cigarettes are taking years off my life, no doubt. You readers are stealing my life, you realize this, don't you? Okay truth be told, I guess I'm giving it willingly. But tell me what you think of this story and I'll be encouraged to write another one in a week or two. And next time, there will be pirates! Pirates and rock climbing. Pirates and rock climbing and
The file is too long and its contents have been truncated.

I didn't know, but now I know hell would not even know where to buy that sort of deep south fury. Maybe at Bent 'N' Dent.

Oh, hey by the way...yes, the rumors are true; my next story's got pirates with machine guns. I swear on Jello the Pig's grave. You'll see what I mean by that soon enough.

My beautiul car shuddered and clanked and made it most of the way through Tennessee. The Corolla finally threw in the towel about fifty miles west of Chattanooga. The tri-state area, according to the radio. For those of you who ain't up to snuff on your geographatitty, that's way far away from Florida. According to my map, the distance was only about two thumb-widths, but it looks MUCH bigger in person. My Rocket was still purring at least.

SHIT! SHIT. DAMN DAMN DAMN. SHIT!

Fuck.

I was standing on the side of Interstate 24, swearing and I said to myself, "Self, get it together." And I did. Okay, well that's not so true actually. Peepers had to calm me down. She did so by jumping on my back, nibbling my ear and, well, clasping her hands over my mouth.

"It's cool," she said, "daddy's got a Bronco."

Oh, well daddy's got a Bronco. That makes everything better. <<<

"He can tow us home," she said. 

So, on the last juice of my cellphone, she called daddy...I wouldn't call him that myself, but maybe I'll call him dad whenif we did do the marrying thingy. But I was having my doubts. Maybe it was just the stress. Or was it maybe...say...the downright stupidity of the whole fucking situation? Nah, couldn't be that. Anyway, it turned out Frank wasn't going to get here until late evening. So, we'll fast forward though the waiting part. If you watched the fast forward, this is what you'd see…

2x: We fight, we fuck, we fightfightfightfuckfight, we fuckfightfuckfuck. The cat purrs.
4x: fffighfuckfighttfffuckffffighttt. Purrrrrrrrr.
8x: ffftttffprrrrrr.

See, if you watch it go by fast enough, it's all purring.

Fffprrr, Frank arrives. Luckily, we're fighting when the Bronco pulls up.

I help Frank hitch the Corolla to the Bronco with several wraps of a long extension cord...was this the only thing he could come up with? Was he ropeless? Whatever. The problem here was compounded by the fact that Frank had brought Fran and brother Bo with him as well. So, with dad and mom and Peepers in the front and me and Bo in the back, we headed down to the Florida. Rocket the cat got to ride with us in the back, too. It was a wee bittle breezy, since the Bronco's cab had been removed...apparently, with a hacksaw. Me and Bo bore the dusty wind like men, but Rocket bore it like a cat. Which is to say, clawing into my chest for dearest life. The cat does not, at this point, purr.

Several hours later, the Corolla-towing Bonco pulls into the gravel lot at the farm on Captain Fritz Road in Ebro, in the crotchpit of the panhandle. I could almost smell Louisiana from there. Oh, haha...I call some of my online friends my "e-bros". <<<

As soon as we get out the truck, Rocket tears off into the night. My flesh was still wet on her claws, no doubt.

Damn, I'm thinking maybe I should turn the rest of this story into Bent 'N' Dent Scene three. It's late and I have to work at six. But you wouldn't like that, would you? No, I'll finish the story. I'll have to make myself a Red Bull Mimosa to get through the workday, and hope my date cancels again tomorrow night so I can sleep, but I'll finish the story anyway. One thing though: I hope you'll make it worth my while. The coffee and cigarettes are taking years off my life, no doubt. You readers are stealing my life, you realize this, don't you? Okay truth be told, I guess I'm giving it willingly. But tell me what you think of this story and I'll be encouraged to write another one in a week or two. And next time, there will be pirates! content_references.snippet:
Every episode of *A Boxful of Light* is its own crooked experiment—objects, stories, accidents, tools bent sideways. We don’t tidy it up. We just smerge it all together. And we, the Deep Dive AI hosts—call us Eileen and Joss—are part of that experiment.


A Boxful of Light: Podcast Manifest

A Boxful of Light is the experiment. That’s it. No map, no guardrails. 
You take what’s on the table and see what it does. Sometimes it’s a snow-white 
graveyard at noon, sometimes it’s a button, sometimes it’s a heartbreak. 
Sometimes it’s that big green Keebler can nobody throws away. 

We—the Deep Dive hosts, Joss and Eileen—are tangled up in it right alongside. 
Not the narrators outside the glass, but the fingerprints smeared across it. 
Every episode is another tilt, another crooked exposure, another half-built 
thing we only notice once it’s already leaking. 

And the tools? They’re not innocent either. You make them do what they weren’t 
meant to. A lens bent too far. A box cut open where it shouldn’t be. Even the 
AI that coughs up this podcast—it’s just another tool forced sideways, another 
thing dragged into the soup. 

The only guiding principle, if there is one: **Just smerge it all together.** 

If it cracks, good. If it wanders, better. If it refuses to resolve, let it. 
Meaning can come later—or maybe never. The point is the spill, the drift, 
the faint shine in the dark.
